output:
Management options:
- Intraoral devices or retainers.
- For acute flares: oral rest, local myofascial release and muscle relaxants.
- Surgery in selected cases.

Dental and periodontal care is complicated by fragile periodontal tissue, poor local anesthetic response, TMJ laxity, craniocervical instability and intolerance of prolonged head and neck positions. Plan procedures accordingly.

instruction: You are a medical educator. Based on the study, are patients with hEDS more severely affected than patients with HSD?
input: We included 97 patients (61 hEDS, 36 HSD). Median age was 40; 92.7% were females. Three items from CSS-16 (pain, motricity problems, and bleeding) were significantly more severe with hEDS than HSD. Bone fragility, neuropathic pain and MCAS were equally prevalent. hEDS and HSD patients showed similar disease severity score except for pain, motricity problems and bleeding, and similar spectrum of extra-articular manifestations. These results add weight to a clinical pragmatic proposition to consider hEDS/HSD as a single entity that requires the same treatments.
output: Only partly. This Swiss study followed 97 patients (61 with hEDS and 36 with HSD; almost 93% women). Those with hEDS had more severe pain, more movement problems and more bleeding issues. But in most other respects the groups were similar, including bone fragility, nerve-type pain and mast cell-related symptoms. The authors conclude that, in everyday practice, it makes sense to treat hEDS and HSD as one group that needs the same kind of care.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A surgeon asks: 'What should I consider before operating on a patient with hEDS?' Answer based on the article.
input: Some individuals will have undergone orthopedic and orthognathic procedures prior to diagnosis. Anecdotally, a lack of awareness of the joint hypermobility and tissue fragility may lead to poorer surgical outcomes, but datasets of outcomes are lacking. Some will require surgical procedures if conservative therapies for hEDS fail or there are significant pathologies present (e.g., impingement disorders, dysplasias, and cord/nerve entrapment with neurologic deficit). Braces and splints are useful to improve alignment and control. They may allow an injured joint to rest and support joints during normal activities and exercising to allow greater duration, frequency, and level of activities.
output:
Points from GeneReviews:
- Many patients have had orthopedic or orthognathic procedures before diagnosis. Anecdotally, unrecognized hypermobility and tissue fragility may lead to poorer outcomes, although outcome data are lacking.
- Conservative therapy (tailored exercise, braces and splints) is first line.
- Surgery is appropriate when conservative care fails or there is significant pathology, such as impingement, dysplasia, or cord or nerve entrapment with neurologic deficit.

Make sure the surgical team is aware of the diagnosis so that hypermobility and tissue fragility can be taken into account.

instruction: You are a health educator. Based on the article, how should people with JHS/hEDS build up exercise or return to sport and dance?
input: Cardiovascular, musculoskeletal and physical fitness training parameters should be encouraged in both children and adults. In general, specialists recommend a carefully graduated exercise training prescription, underpinned by motor learning theory, to avoid injury and overtraining as this may lead to loss of confidence in the physical therapist. Pain, fatigue, and fear of injury are commonly reported barriers to exercise. A graduated return to higher levels of sport or dance is recommended, and training loads should be observed to ensure adequate recovery.
output: Fitness training—for the heart, muscles and overall condition—is encouraged for both children and adults with JHS/hEDS. The key is to build up gradually, so you avoid injury and overtraining, which can also damage your confidence in therapy. Pain, tiredness and fear of getting hurt are common reasons people struggle to exercise, so a step-by-step plan helps. If you want to return to sport or dance, do it gradually and keep an eye on your training load so your body has enough time to recover.

instruction: You are a health educator. Based on the review, is hEDS really as rare as people think?
input: EDS as a whole has been estimated to impact 1 in 5,000 people worldwide, however, there is limited evidence to support this statistic. Demmler et al recently reported the combined prevalence of hEDS and HSD to be 1 in 500 people in Wales with 70% of the diagnosed being women, suggesting that hEDS/HSD prevalence has been grossly underestimated. With the spectrum of severity, variation in symptom presentation and the lack of an effective clinical diagnostic test, it is not uncommon for patients to go years undiagnosed with hEDS. Because of this, it can be assumed that the actual prevalence of hEDS is higher than reported.
output: Probably not. The often-quoted figure of 1 in 5,000 people for all types of EDS has little evidence behind it. A study in Wales found that hEDS and hypermobility spectrum disorders together were diagnosed in about 1 in 500 people—70% of them women—suggesting these conditions have been greatly underestimated. Because symptoms vary so much and there is no diagnostic test, many people go years without a diagnosis, so the true number is likely even higher than reported.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'Many of my hypermobile patients seem distrustful and anxious at appointments. How can I communicate effectively with them?' Answer based on the articles.
input: Source 1 (GeneReviews): Validation of symptoms can be immensely helpful, as many with hEDS have been accused by health care professionals of malingering or diagnosed with primary psychiatric disorders. Establishing trust, rapport, and a supportive relationship with the affected individual is important. Anxiety and depression are a common result of the many morbidities a person with hEDS may experience. Source 2 (Halverson et al.): Many individuals have had their symptoms dismissed as psychosomatic. Such dismissal has critical negative consequences for the patient's psychological and physical well-being, potentially leading to a delayed diagnosis, the prescription of unnecessary antipsychotics, and the development of long-lasting trauma responses to otherwise benign clinical encounters. Patients saw an average of 15.6 clinicians and the average time to diagnosis was 10.39 years. Source 3 (Anderson & Lane): Anger and frustration with providers can lead people with hEDS/HSD to avoid health care encounters. Many providers did not know that chronic widespread pain was a common hEDS/HSD characteristic.
output:
Context helps. Patients with hEDS see an average of about 15.6 clinicians and wait about 10 years for a diagnosis. Many have been told their symptoms were psychosomatic or have been accused of malingering, and some respond by avoiding care altogether. Wariness at appointments is often a learned response to these encounters.

Practical approaches drawn from the articles:
- Validate early. Acknowledge that pain, fatigue and multisystem symptoms are recognized features of hEDS/HSD. This alone can be very helpful.
- Build trust and continuity. A consistent clinician who coordinates care reduces fragmentation.
- Address mental health without dismissal. Anxiety and depression are common consequences of the condition, and they can be treated alongside, not instead of, the physical symptoms.
- Avoid premature psychiatric labelling. Unwarranted labels have led to delayed diagnosis, unnecessary antipsychotic prescriptions and lasting medical trauma.
- Believe procedural pain reports. Reduced response to local anesthetics is common, and disbelief during procedures has been a source of harm.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'Which clinical manifestations are associated with hEDS even though they are not part of the 2017 diagnostic criteria?' Answer based on the article.
input: hEDS is associated with clinical manifestations that are not included in the published diagnostic criteria including: chronic fatigue; easy bruising; functional bowel disorders (gastroesophageal reflux, gastritis, early satiety, delayed gastric emptying, irritable bowel syndrome, constipation); additional cardiovascular manifestations (autonomic dysfunction, Raynaud phenomenon, acrocyanosis); reduced efficacy of local anesthetics; laryngeal and breathing disorders including apnea; neurologic complications (migraine, Chiari I malformation, cerebrospinal fluid leaks, craniocervical instability, tethered cord, entrapment and peripheral neuropathy, small fiber neuropathy); mast cell activation disorders and immune deficiency; anxiety disorders; autism and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder; urogynecologic manifestations (dysmenorrhea, menorrhagia, interstitial cystitis, urinary incontinence, pelvic organ prolapse).

instruction: A patient asks: 'Why are most people with hEDS women if it is inherited equally?' Answer based on the article.
input: hEDS is considered to be an autosomal dominant trait with variable expressivity. Yet, many studies point out a strong excess of affected females, at least in adults. The ratio ranges from 8-9:1 to ~2:1, depending upon how patients are selected. In early childhood, the male to female ratio of affected is similar. However, in the general population, as children enter puberty, joint mobility tends to increase in females and decrease in males. The reason for the sex bias remains incompletely understood with speculation of a greater influence of female sex hormones. hEDS is best defined as an autosomal disorder 'influenced by sex', with a predominance of symptoms in females.
output: That is a great question, and researchers don't fully know the answer yet. hEDS is passed on in a way that should affect boys and girls equally, and in early childhood the numbers are indeed similar. But in adults many more women are affected, with ratios reported from about 2:1 up to 8-9:1 depending on how patients are counted. One clue is puberty: at that age joint flexibility tends to increase in girls and decrease in boys, and female sex hormones are thought to play a role. Most chronic pain conditions are also more common in women. This is why experts describe hEDS as a condition 'influenced by sex', with symptoms that are more common and often more severe in females.

instruction: You are a health educator specializing in hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS). Based on the article, explain in simple terms what hEDS is.
input: The hypermobile type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS) is likely the most common hereditary disorder of connective tissue. It has been described largely in those with musculoskeletal complaints including joint hypermobility, joint subluxations/dislocations, as well as skin and soft tissue manifestations. Many patients report activity-related pain and some go on to have daily pain.
output: Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS) is an inherited condition that affects connective tissue—the 'glue' that holds joints, skin and organs together. It is probably the most common inherited connective tissue disorder. People with hEDS usually have very flexible joints that can partially slip out of place (subluxations) or fully dislocate, along with softer, slightly stretchy skin. Many people feel pain during or after activity, and for some this develops into pain that is present every day.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. An anesthetist asks: 'How should I plan obstetric anesthesia for a woman with hEDS who reports local anesthetic resistance?' Answer based on the case series.
input: Although the majority had a definite history of resistance to local anaesthetics (previous dental procedures), regional blockade for pain relief in labour/caesarean section was found to be effective in these women. One woman required more frequent top-up with local anaesthetics for epidural for effective pain relief in labour. A multi-disciplinary approach was adopted in the management of these women in pregnancy, including anaesthetic consultation and where required referral to the pain management team, physiotherapy and cardiology.
output:
In this case series, most women had a history of poor response to local anesthetics, mostly from dental procedures. Even so, regional blockade (epidural or spinal) was effective for labor analgesia and caesarean section. One woman needed more frequent epidural top-ups.

Practical points:
- A history of resistance should not preclude regional anesthesia.
- Anticipate higher or more frequent dosing.
- Arrange an antenatal anesthetic consultation as part of multidisciplinary care, together with pain management, physiotherapy and cardiology where needed.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'Which factors contribute to diagnostic delay in hEDS/HSD?' Answer based on the review.
input: The reviewers identified and organized diagnosis delay themes under four overarching categories: disease, patient, provider, and system. Disease factors included the nature of the symptoms and lack of a confirmatory test. Patient factors included psychological and emotional responses, seeing multiple providers, and receiving multiple diagnoses. Provider factors related to limited knowledge and attitudes. System factors included silo-based health care systems and bureaucratic barriers.
output:
The review grouped the factors into four categories:
- Disease: variable, nonspecific symptoms and no confirmatory test.
- Patient: psychological and emotional responses, seeing multiple providers and receiving multiple diagnoses.
- Provider: limited knowledge and negative attitudes.
- System: siloed health care and bureaucratic barriers.

Identifying which factors apply in your setting, for example missing referral pathways or training gaps, can help target improvements.

instruction: A patient with hEDS asks: 'Will supplements like CoQ10 or magnesium help my fatigue?' Answer based on the article.
input: There is insufficient evidence to recommend the use of complementary therapies and supplements for fatigue. However, some patients choose to use these therapies and find them helpful, and there is little evidence of harm. Typical agents include co-enzyme Q10, Carnitine, alpha-lipoic acid, magnesium, NADH, and multivitamins and minerals. Co-enzyme Q and Riboflavin have been shown to be effective in migraine prophylaxis. In some cases, patients with bowel dysfunction may need supplements because of a restricted diet. Unless there is an underlying medical disorder, the following medications should be avoided as they may cause harm: glucocorticoids, thyroxine (in the absence of hypothyroidism), antiviral agents (in the absence of confirmed active viral infection).
output: There isn't enough evidence to recommend supplements such as coenzyme Q10, carnitine, alpha-lipoic acid, magnesium, NADH or multivitamins for fatigue. Some people try them and feel they help, and they appear to carry little risk. Coenzyme Q10 and riboflavin do have evidence for preventing migraines. If gut problems restrict your diet, you may genuinely need supplements, ideally guided by a dietitian. The article also warns against some treatments without a clear medical reason: steroids, thyroid hormone if your thyroid is normal, and antiviral drugs without a confirmed active infection, as these may cause harm. Let your doctor know about anything you take.

instruction: You are a health educator answering a patient's question. Based on the article, how common is hEDS?
input: Accurate prevalence estimation studies are still lacking for hEDS. Steinmann et al. reported a minimum prevalence of 1/5,000 for all types of EDS collectively. As hEDS likely represents 80-90% of cases of EDS, the prevalence is presumed not lower than 1/5,000. A much higher prevalence of 7.5/1,000 to 20/1,000 (0.75-2%) for 'symptomatic' GJH has been proposed, considering that about 10% of individuals with GJH may develop related symptoms in their lifetime. However, the diagnostic criteria proposed herein are more selective, so the prevalence of hEDS under these criteria may be somewhat lower than some of these estimates.
output: Nobody knows the exact number yet, because good population studies are still missing. Ehlers-Danlos syndromes as a whole affect at least 1 in 5,000 people, and since hEDS makes up roughly 80-90% of all EDS cases, hEDS is thought to affect at least that many. Some researchers estimate that symptomatic joint hypermobility may affect 0.75-2% of people, because about 1 in 10 people with very flexible joints develop related symptoms during their life. Under the stricter 2017 criteria the true number of people with hEDS may be somewhat lower than these higher estimates.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'How should I prescribe graded exercise for a patient with hEDS and fatigue?' Answer based on the article.
input: A suitably trained therapist or instructor should deliver GET. Recommendations such as 'go to the gym', 'exercise more', or 'go swimming' are not helpful without supported advice on what this actually means, and should be avoided. It is recommended that exercise should be supervised, structured, and gradually increased in intensity. Unstructured and unsupervised exercise may worsen symptoms, as can a rigid or inflexible escalation of activity. When planning GET, it is important clinicians and/or therapists: undertake an assessment of current activity; discuss both short and long-term goals; agree on a level of additional low-intensity exercise that is sustainable; recognize that it can take weeks, months, or even years to achieve goals; advise that increased levels of exercise may increase symptoms for a few days (e.g., stiffness and fatigue), but explain that this is normal.
output:
Avoid unstructured advice such as 'go to the gym' or 'go swimming'. Exercise should be supervised by a suitably trained therapist, structured, and progressed gradually but flexibly. Unsupervised exercise or rigid escalation can worsen symptoms.

Steps:
1. Assess current activity without triggering boom-and-bust cycles.
2. Agree short- and long-term goals that matter to the patient.
3. Add sustainable low-intensity exercise.
4. Warn that a few days of increased stiffness or fatigue after progression is normal.
5. Plan for setbacks and long-term maintenance.

Goals may take weeks, months or even years to reach, and the therapy structure should allow for this.

instruction: You are a health educator explaining digestive problems in hEDS. Based on the article, what gut symptoms are common and how are they evaluated?
input: Collectively, functional features may be observed in 1/3 to 3/4 of the patients with an increasing rate by age. Manifestations variably include gastroesophageal reflux, heartburn, bloating, recurrent abdominal pain, irritable bowel syndrome, constipation, and diarrhea. Constipation with or without other features of voiding dysfunction is usually the earliest sign of gastrointestinal involvement. Standard investigations are usually carried out without severe complications in hEDS, but they often have negative or inconsistent results. Treatment of functional GI complaints in hEDS is problematic due to the absence of tailored strategies and an apparent resistance to pharmacologic treatments at standard dosages. The exclusion of common comorbidities, such as celiac disease, lactose intolerance, and Helicobacter pylori infection, is reasonable at first examination.
output: Digestive problems are very common in hEDS—between one-third and three-quarters of patients have them, and they become more frequent with age. Typical complaints include acid reflux and heartburn, bloating, recurring tummy pain, irritable bowel syndrome, constipation and diarrhea. Constipation is often the first sign that the gut is involved. Standard tests are usually safe in hEDS but frequently come back normal or inconclusive. A sensible first step is to check for common treatable conditions such as celiac disease, lactose intolerance and Helicobacter pylori infection. Treatment can be challenging because there are no hEDS-specific approaches yet, and some people respond less well to usual medication doses.

instruction: A patient with hEDS asks: 'I often feel I can't fully empty my bowels. Is there a test for that?' Answer based on the expert review.
input: Diagnostic testing for functional defecation disorders with anorectal manometry, balloon expulsion test, or defecography should be considered in patients with hEDS/HSDs and lower GI symptoms such as incomplete evacuation given the high prevalence of pelvic floor dysfunction, especially rectal hyposensitivity, in this population.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A rehabilitation clinician asks: 'Some patients with JHS/hEDS rely on family for daily tasks. What does the research suggest for rehabilitation?' Answer based on the study.
input: Participants who had help from family members to complete activities described guilt and shame, highlighting the need for a greater rehabilitation focus on maintaining independence. One male participant stated, 'Sometimes I feel a burden, or a nuisance… that's why I end up… having the anxiety problems… feeling sorry for other people, having to put up with me'. Coping approaches identified included acceptance, building social networks, learning about joint hypermobility and adapting activities.
output:
Participants who relied on family members described guilt and shame. One described feeling like 'a burden, or a nuisance', which fed his anxiety. The authors conclude that rehabilitation needs a greater focus on maintaining independence.

Coping strategies that helped were acceptance, building social networks, learning about hypermobility and adapting activities.

In practice, include independence-focused goals, occupational therapy and activity adaptation, and address the psychological burden of dependence.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'What treatment options exist for POTS or neurally mediated hypotension in hEDS?' Answer based on the article.
input: Cardiovascular. Standard treatments for neurally mediated hypotension and postural orthostatic tachycardia are advised, including avoidance of sudden postural change, consideration of lower extremity and/or abdominal compression garments, exercise to increase muscle strength and improve tone, supplementation of sodium and water to expand the blood volume, and sometimes pharmacologic treatment with beta-blockers, midodrine, fludrocortisone, ivabradine, and/or other medications initiated by a clinician experienced in autonomic medicine. Commercially available electrolyte tablets can facilitate oral expansion of blood volume.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'What should I tell a patient about the inheritance and genetics of hEDS?' Answer based on the article.
input: hEDS, for the most part, is inherited as an autosomal dominant disorder of connective tissue but other patterns of inheritance can be seen in some families; however, this may be confounded by non-penetrance, sex-influence as well as genetic heterogeneity. Unfortunately, unlike the other types of EDS, hEDS has no known genetic etiology responsible for any significant portion of this population. JH itself is multifactorial with age, gender, weight, training, and other aspects that influence this phenotype. Twin studies have determined that the concordance of JH among dizygotic twins was 36% in 472 female twin pairs, whereas monozygotic twins had a concordance rate of 60% in 483 female twin pairs suggesting a strong genetic trait with multifactorial influences.
output:
Key points to convey:
- hEDS is usually inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. Non-penetrance, sex influence and genetic heterogeneity can obscure the pattern in a given family.
- Unlike other EDS types, there is no known gene that explains a significant proportion of cases, so no confirmatory genetic test exists.
- Joint hypermobility itself is multifactorial and influenced by age, sex, weight and training. Twin data support a strong genetic component, with 60% concordance in monozygotic female twins versus 36% in dizygotic twins.

The diagnosis therefore remains clinical. Genetic testing is used to exclude other conditions, not to confirm hEDS.

instruction: You are a medical educator. Based on the study, what did heart ultrasounds show in people with classical and hypermobile EDS?
input: We have examined a cohort of 38 patients with hypermobile and classical EDSs using two-dimensional echocardiography. Five of the 38 participants had mildly dilated aortic root or sinuses of Valsalva, and an additional 7 patients had an abnormal pouching of the sinuses of Valsalva, although the absolute dimensions did not exceed the normal range. Ten patients had mild mitral, tricuspid, or aortic regurgitation, and only one patient had mitral valve prolapse. The 'pouching' shape of the sinuses of Valsalva was more common in hypermobile type than in the classical type of EDS.
output: Researchers performed heart ultrasounds (echocardiograms) on 38 people with classical or hypermobile EDS. Most findings were mild: 5 people had a slightly widened aortic root (the beginning of the main artery), and 7 more—all with hypermobile EDS—had an unusual 'pouch-like' shape of the aortic root even though its size was normal. Ten people had mild leaking of a heart valve, and only one person met the criteria for mitral valve prolapse. Overall, the study found mostly subtle changes rather than serious heart disease, and the researchers planned to follow patients over time to see whether these changes progress.

instruction: A patient with POTS asks: 'Should I be checked for hEDS?' Answer based on the study.
input: We therefore evaluated for hEDS in 91 POTS participants using the 2017 hEDS diagnostic checklist, which has three major criteria: 1) generalized joint hypermobility (Beighton score), 2) systemic features, family history, and 3) absence of exclusion criteria. Overall, 28 out of 91 POTS participants (31%) met clinical criteria for hEDS. An additional 24% of participants had generalized joint hypermobility without meeting hEDS criteria.
output: It may be worth asking your doctor. In this study, physicians examined 91 people with POTS using the official 2017 hEDS checklist. Nearly a third (31%) met the full criteria for hEDS, and another 24% had generalized joint hypermobility without meeting all the hEDS criteria. So more than half of the participants had significant hypermobility. If you also have very flexible joints, joint pain or dislocations, or relatives with similar problems, an assessment for hEDS could help explain your symptoms and guide your care.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'When should I suspect MCAS in a patient with hEDS, and how do I test for it?' Answer based on the AGA expert review.
input: Best Practice Advice 5: Testing for mast cell disorders including MCAS should be considered in patients with hEDS/HSDs and DGBI who also present with episodic symptoms that suggest a more generalized mast cell disorder (eg, visceral and somatic pain, pruritus, flushing, sweating, urticaria, angioedema, wheezing, tachycardia, abdominal cramping, vomiting, nausea, diarrhea, urogynecological and neurological complaints) involving 2 or more physiological systems (eg, cutaneous, GI, cardiac, respiratory, and neuropsychiatric), but current data do not support the use of these tests for routine evaluation of GI symptoms in all patients with hEDS/HSDs without clinical or laboratory evidence of a primary or secondary mast cell disorder. Best Practice Advice 6: If MCAS is suspected, diagnostic testing with serum tryptase levels collected at baseline and 1–4 hours following symptom flares may be considered; increases of 20% above baseline plus 2 ng/mL are necessary to demonstrate evidence of mast cell activation. Best Practice Advice 7: If a diagnosis of MCAS is supported through clinical and/or laboratory features, patients should be referred to an allergy specialist or mast cell disease research center where additional testing (eg, urinary N-methylhistamine, leukotriene E4, 11β-prostaglandin F2) may be performed.
output:
When to suspect it: episodic symptoms involving two or more organ systems. Examples include flushing, pruritus, urticaria or angioedema (skin); cramping, nausea, vomiting or diarrhea (GI); tachycardia; wheezing; and neuropsychiatric or urogynecological complaints. The AGA does not support routine mast-cell testing for GI symptoms in all patients with hEDS/HSD.

How to test:
- Measure serum tryptase at baseline and again 1–4 hours after a symptomatic flare.
- Mast cell activation is supported by a rise of at least 20% above baseline plus 2 ng/mL. For example, with a baseline of 5 ng/mL the threshold is 8 ng/mL (5 × 1.2 + 2).

Next step: if clinical or laboratory features support MCAS, refer to allergy/immunology or a mast cell center for further tests such as urinary N-methylhistamine, leukotriene E4 and 11β-prostaglandin F2.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A neurologist asks: 'What does formal autonomic and small-fiber testing typically show in hEDS?' Answer based on the study.
input: Total 270 hEDS patients were analyzed and compared to 29 healthy controls. Common hEDS complaints (prevalence >90%) were orthostatic, sudomotor, vasomotor, gastrointestinal, and pain. Orthostatic cerebral blood flow velocity was reduced in 79% of hEDS and correlated with orthostatic dizziness. The head-up tilt test revealed postural tachycardia syndrome (prevalence 33%), hypocapnic cerebral hypoperfusion (22%), orthostatic cerebral hypoperfusion syndrome (18%), and neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (9%). Widespread but mild autonomic failure was present in 90% of hEDS patients on autonomic testing. Small fiber neuropathy using structural criteria was detected in 64%, and using combined structural and functional criteria in 82%. The most significant finding of this study is the presence of cerebrovascular dysregulation associated with reduced cerebral blood flow that can result in cerebral hypoperfusion, orthostatic intolerance, and impaired well-being. This is a potentially modifiable treatment target. Our study provides additional evidence that SFN is an underlying cause of both dysautonomia and certain types of chronic pain in hEDS.
output:
In a large retrospective series (270 patients with hEDS who underwent autonomic testing and skin biopsy, compared with 29 controls):

- Symptoms: orthostatic, sudomotor, vasomotor, GI and pain complaints were each reported by more than 90%.
- Cerebral blood flow: orthostatic cerebral blood flow velocity was reduced in 79% and correlated with orthostatic dizziness.
- Tilt test: POTS in 33%, hypocapnic cerebral hypoperfusion in 22%, orthostatic cerebral hypoperfusion syndrome in 18%, neurogenic orthostatic hypotension in 9%.
- Autonomic function: widespread but mild autonomic failure in 90%.
- Small-fiber neuropathy: 64% on skin biopsy alone, 82% when structural and functional criteria were combined.

Clinical relevance:
- Dizziness, brain fog and orthostatic intolerance may reflect cerebral hypoperfusion even without classic POTS, so tilt testing with cerebral blood flow and capnography can be informative.
- Small-fiber neuropathy is common and may underlie both dysautonomia and part of the chronic pain, so consider skin biopsy when neuropathic symptoms are present.

The authors see cerebral hypoperfusion as a potentially modifiable treatment target, although pharmacological options need further study.

instruction: You are a medical educator. Based on the review, what are the three main challenges researchers and clinicians face with chronic pain in HMS/EDS-HT, and what solutions do the authors propose?
input: Researchers and clinicians have struggled for decades with the highly diverse clinical presentation within the HMS and EDS-HT phenotypes (Challenge 1) and the lack of understanding of the pathological mechanisms that underlie the development of pain and its persistence (Challenge 2). In addition, within the HMS/EDS-HT phenotype, there is a high prevalence of psychosocial factors, which again presents a difficult issue that needs to be addressed (Challenge 3). Future research and clinical care should revise and create consensus on the diagnostic criteria for HMS/EDS-HT (Solution 1), account for clinical heterogeneity by the classification of subtypes within the HMS/EDS-HT spectrum (Solution 2), and create a clinical core set (Solution 3).
output: The authors describe three challenges. First, symptoms vary enormously from person to person, so patients can look very different. Second, we still don't understand well why pain develops and why it persists. Third, psychosocial factors such as stress, anxiety or fear of movement are very common and need to be addressed too. Their proposed solutions are: agree on clearer, shared diagnostic criteria; recognize different subtypes within the spectrum to account for this variety; and create a 'core set'—a standard group of measurements that all clinicians and researchers use, so results can be compared.

instruction: You are a medical educator. Based on the review, why might people with hEDS/HSD have gastrointestinal symptoms?
input: The pathophysiology of gut symptoms is poorly understood but may involve effects of connective tissue laxity and its functional consequences, and the influence of autonomic dysfunction, medication and comorbid mental health disorders. Awareness is the key to early diagnosis. Management is limited in evidence-base but ideally should include an integrated multidisciplinary approach.
output: The exact reasons are not yet well understood, but several factors probably play a role together: looser connective tissue in and around the gut, which may affect how it moves and works; problems with the autonomic nervous system, which controls digestion automatically; side effects of medicines such as painkillers; and coexisting anxiety or depression, which can influence gut function through the gut-brain connection. Because the evidence for specific treatments is still limited, the best approach is coordinated care from a team of professionals, and recognizing hEDS early helps.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A pediatrician asks: 'Are urinary problems more common in hypermobile children?' Answer based on the article.
input: De Kort et al. evaluated 89 families of children with GJH. The children with GJH showed an increase in daytime and nighttime urinary incontinence as well as urinary tract infections (UTIs). Voiding dysfunction was also significantly associated with GJH in children but this is unclear if this is secondary to constipation. Adib et al. evaluated 125 children with a diagnosis of hEDS and catalogued their multisystem disorders. UTIs and urinary tract dysfunction were more common in girls than controls. Vesicoureteral reflux was also more common in children with hEDS as compared to the control population.
output:
Yes. Reported findings:
- Children with generalized hypermobility (89 families studied) had more daytime and night-time incontinence and more urinary tract infections.
- Voiding dysfunction was significantly associated with hypermobility, although it may be secondary to constipation.
- In 125 children with hEDS, UTIs and urinary tract dysfunction were more common in girls than in controls, and vesicoureteral reflux was more common than in controls.

In hypermobile children with recurrent UTIs or incontinence, assess bowel habits for constipation and have a low threshold for evaluating for reflux.

instruction: A newly diagnosed patient asks: 'What can I do about my mood and anxiety? Some doctors made me feel it was all in my head.' Answer with empathy based on the article.
input: Neurobehavioral/psychiatric manifestations. Validation of symptoms can be immensely helpful, as many with hEDS have been accused by health care professionals of malingering or diagnosed with primary psychiatric disorders. Establishing trust, rapport, and a supportive relationship with the affected individual is important. Anxiety and depression are a common result of the many morbidities a person with hEDS may experience. Psychological and/or symptom-oriented counseling can improve adaptation to and acceptance of these issues and their impact on quality of life. Cognitive behavioral therapy can be beneficial but requires active participation. Antidepressants may also be of benefit.
output: I'm sorry you went through that—many people with hEDS have been told their symptoms were imagined or purely psychiatric. Now that you have a diagnosis, your physical symptoms are recognized as real. At the same time, anxiety and depression are common consequences of living with many symptoms, and they deserve care too. The article notes that being believed and having a trusting relationship with clinicians helps a lot. Counseling focused on your symptoms can help you adapt to and accept the changes in your life, cognitive behavioral therapy can help if you take an active part in it, and antidepressants may also be useful. Seeking psychological support doesn't mean your problems are 'in your head'—it's one part of treating the whole person.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A pediatric physiotherapist asks: 'What affects adherence to home exercise programs in children with JHS/hEDS?' Answer based on the article.
input: Qualitative interviews with 28 families with children with JHS/hEDS (5-17 years) on prerequisites for the best adherence to exercise is reported to be parental motivation adapting family routines, making exercise a family activity and seeing the benefit. On the other hand are factors for non-adherence to exercise for these children, lower levels of parental supervision, not understanding the treatment, not seeing the benefit and not having specific time to dedicate for doing exercises.

instruction: A patient asks: 'Why have I been given so many different diagnoses for my symptoms?' Answer based on the article.
input: Patients with hEDS/HSD experience many individual symptoms over time, never suspecting a possible connection between them. As a result, patients may have multiple health care encounters and receive multiple diagnoses, including postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, irritable bowel syndrome, fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue syndrome/myalgic encephalopathy, and spinal pathologies. 'In some cases, they spend many years until a diagnostic label is assigned to all the symptomology…they accumulate a number of diagnoses specific to each symptom'. However, in some cases, investigation of another illness eventually led to the hEDS/HSD diagnosis. For example, one participant stated, 'My hypermobility has been identified as a result of investigations into my chronic IBS'.
output: This happens to many people with hEDS/HSD. Symptoms appear over the years in different parts of the body, and neither patients nor doctors always see the connection. Each symptom may get its own label—for example POTS, irritable bowel syndrome, fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue syndrome or a back problem. Some of these may be real coexisting conditions; others may later be better explained by hEDS. Sometimes one of these investigations is exactly what leads to the right diagnosis—one person's hypermobility was discovered while doctors were investigating their chronic IBS.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'How can I support a patient with hEDS and severe fatigue to stay in work or education?' Answer based on the article.
input: Disruption of education or employment is generally detrimental to health and wellbeing. The ability to continue in these should be addressed early. The clinician should assist, following consent from their patient, by proactively and as needs be regularly advising colleagues on their patients' fitness for work and education, and the adjustments or adaptations required for them to remain in or return to studies or work. For people with moderate or severe fatigue that has not responded to treatment, equipment and adaptations (e.g., a wheelchair) should be considered as part of the management plan. Such adaptations may be valued ways of gaining more independence and improving quality of life. The clinician should support applications for financial benefits and social care.
output:
Disruption of education or employment is generally detrimental to health, so address it early. With consent:
- Proactively advise employers, schools or occupational health on fitness for work or study.
- Recommend adjustments or adaptations needed to remain in, or return to, work or education.
- Review these regularly.

Also support applications for financial benefits and social care. For moderate to severe fatigue unresponsive to treatment, consider equipment and adaptations, such as a wheelchair, after a risk-benefit assessment, because they can increase independence and quality of life.

instruction: You are a medical educator. Based on the case series, how did local and regional anesthesia work in pregnant women with hEDS?
input: Although the majority had a definite history of resistance to local anaesthetics (previous dental procedures), regional blockade for pain relief in labour/caesarean section was found to be effective in these women. One woman required more frequent top-up with local anaesthetics for epidural for effective pain relief in labour. A multi-disciplinary approach was adopted in the management of these women in pregnancy, including anaesthetic consultation and where required referral to the pain management team, physiotherapy and cardiology.
output: Most women in this case series had noticed before that local anesthetics didn't work well for them—for example at the dentist. Even so, regional anesthesia (an epidural or spinal block) gave effective pain relief during labor or caesarean section; one woman simply needed more frequent epidural top-ups. This is reassuring, and it shows why it helps to meet the anesthetic team during pregnancy, as these women did, alongside other specialists when needed.

instruction: You are a medical educator. Based on the article, which 'red flag' signs suggest that fatigue in someone with hEDS might be caused by a different, serious condition?
input: It is important to recognize that chronic fatigue may be the result of a co-existing condition. 'Red flag' alerts of a serious different condition include: weight loss, significant lymphadenopathy, clubbing, persistent shortness of breath on exertion, fevers, red swollen joints, bronzing of the skin, abnormalities on the neurological examination, later age of onset. The following should then be excluded or investigated further: chronic infection, endocrine disorders (e.g., diabetes, thyroid disease, adrenal insufficiency), autoimmune inflammatory conditions, cardiorespiratory disease, sleep disordered breathing, neurological disorders.
output: Having hEDS doesn't mean all fatigue is caused by hEDS. The article lists warning signs that should prompt a search for another condition: unexplained weight loss, noticeably swollen lymph nodes, clubbing of the fingertips, ongoing shortness of breath with exertion, fevers, red and swollen joints, bronze-colored skin, abnormal findings on a neurological exam, or fatigue that starts later in life. In such cases doctors should check for chronic infections, hormone problems (such as diabetes, thyroid or adrenal disease), autoimmune conditions, heart or lung disease, breathing problems during sleep and neurological disorders. If you notice any of these signs, see your doctor.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'Is the 1 in 5,000 prevalence figure for EDS still accurate?' Answer based on the review.
input: EDS as a whole has been estimated to impact 1 in 5,000 people worldwide, however, there is limited evidence to support this statistic. Demmler et al recently reported the combined prevalence of hEDS and HSD to be 1 in 500 people in Wales with 70% of the diagnosed being women, suggesting that hEDS/HSD prevalence has been grossly underestimated. With the spectrum of severity, variation in symptom presentation and the lack of an effective clinical diagnostic test, it is not uncommon for patients to go years undiagnosed with hEDS. Because of this, it can be assumed that the actual prevalence of hEDS is higher than reported.
output:
Probably not for hEDS and HSD. The 1 in 5,000 estimate for all EDS has limited supporting evidence. A Welsh population study found a combined diagnosed prevalence of hEDS and HSD of about 1 in 500, 70% of them women, which suggests substantial underestimation.

Variable severity and presentation, and the lack of a diagnostic test, mean many patients go undiagnosed for years, so true prevalence is likely higher still. Hypermobility-related disorders are therefore not rare in clinical practice.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'What headache types should I consider in a patient with hEDS?' Answer based on the article.
input: Migraines were seen at a greater frequency and disability compared to a control population. Headache due to CSF leak has been demonstrated in a few case reports and affects a very small minority of hEDS patients but can cause significant disability. Craniocervical junction instability is thought to be linked to cervicogenic and Chiari-like headaches. This instability or simply the musculature strain throughout the upper body can cause widespread spasms and muscular tension leading to headaches as well. Temporal headaches may be related to muscular dysfunction involving the temporomandibular joint. Those patients with dysautonomia, orthostatic intolerance, or POTS can also complain of intense pounding headaches. Medications and medication-overuse can also be responsible for headaches in this population. Individual patients often suffer from more than one type of headache.
output:
Several headache types occur, and many patients have more than one:
- Migraine: more frequent and more disabling than in controls.
- Cervicogenic or tension-type headache: from muscle strain and spasm. Craniocervical instability is thought to be linked to cervicogenic and Chiari-like headaches.
- Temporal headache: may relate to muscular dysfunction involving the TMJ.
- Orthostatic, pounding headache: in patients with POTS or orthostatic intolerance.
- CSF leak headache: affects a very small minority but can be disabling.
- Medication-overuse headache.

Because mechanisms overlap, take a careful history of each headache pattern before choosing treatment.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'What are common pitfalls when performing the Beighton score?' Answer based on the article.
input: Passive dorsiflexion of each fifth finger greater than 90 degrees. This should be assessed with the palm and forearm resting on a flat surface and is considered positive only if the fifth metacarpal-phalangeal joint (MCP) can be extended more than 90 degrees. Ability to extend the tip of the fifth finger to a position proximal to the MCP is insufficient to be called positive if the MCP does not extend more than 90 degrees. Hyperextension of each knee greater than 10 degrees should be measured with a goniometer, with the individual standing and knees fully extended. Ability to place the palms flat on the floor is considered positive only if the total palm of both hands lies flat on the floor just in front of the feet. Slight flexion of the knees, spreading of the feet, failure to get the heels of the palms to the floor, and positioning the hands more than a few inches in front of the feet are common causes of false positive scoring of this point. Note: individuals with a positive 5PQ but scoring two or more points below the age-specific Beighton cutoff should be assessed further outside of the Beighton score (e.g., shoulders, hips, ankles, toes) for evidence of generalized joint hypermobility.
output:
Common sources of error:

- Fifth finger: test with the palm and forearm flat on a table. Score it only if the MCP joint itself extends beyond 90°. A fingertip that reaches past the MCP line without true MCP hyperextension does not count.
- Elbows and knees: measure hyperextension above 10° with a goniometer rather than estimating by eye. Assess the knees standing, with the knees fully extended.
- Forward flexion: the knees must be locked and the feet together, and the whole palms must rest flat on the floor just in front of the feet. Slightly flexed knees, feet apart, the heels of the hands lifted, or hands placed several inches forward are frequent causes of false positives.

Also remember that the Beighton score samples only a few joints. If the 5PQ is positive but the score is two or more points below the age-specific cut-off, examine other joints (shoulders, hips, ankles, toes) before concluding that generalized hypermobility is absent.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'Are there medications or interventions I should be cautious about in patients with hEDS?' Answer based on the article.
input: High-impact activity may increase the risk for acute subluxation/dislocation and acute and chronic pain. Most sports and activities are acceptable with appropriate precautions. Chiropractic adjustment and yoga are not contraindicated but must be performed in ways that avoid subluxations or dislocations. Autonomic concerns, gastrointestinal disorders, and intolerances, for example, may preclude use of medications or their excipients (e.g., common analgesics in someone with slow gastrointestinal transit, vasodilator in a person with orthostatic intolerance). Topical agents and adhesives should be used cautiously in those with skin fragility and/or allergy. Many individuals have a poor response to local anesthetic that requires additional doses throughout dental procedures or other analgesia. Platelet disorders may respond to tranexamic or mefenamic acid. For severe bleeding or operative prophylaxis, desmopressin acetate (DDAVP) may be beneficial. Medications that diminish platelet function should generally be avoided in patients with hypermobile EDS who have easy bruising.
output:
Practical cautions from the sources:

- Comorbidity-driven prescribing: drugs that slow GI transit (including many common analgesics) can worsen dysmotility, and vasodilators can worsen orthostatic intolerance or POTS. Patients may also react to excipients, so review formulations in those with known intolerances.
- Bleeding: avoid antiplatelet-effect drugs in patients who bruise easily. Tranexamic acid or mefenamic acid may help platelet-type bleeding, and desmopressin can be considered for severe bleeding or surgical prophylaxis.
- Skin: use adhesives and topical agents cautiously when the skin is fragile or the patient is allergic.
- Local anesthesia: reduced efficacy is common. Plan for additional doses or alternative analgesia during procedures, and believe patients who report feeling pain.
- Physical interventions: high-impact activity raises the risk of dislocation. Manipulation, chiropractic care and yoga are not contraindicated but should avoid end-range forces that could cause subluxation.

instruction: You are a medical educator discussing extra-articular features or traits associated with joint conditions. Did the study look at dental braces in hypermobile individuals?
input: When participants were asked about dental braces statistically significant difference was found between generalized joint hypermobility or hypermobile EDS and participants with a Beighton scoring of 0/9. The prevalences of participants with dental braces in the hypermobile EDS and non-hypermobile EDS groups were 44% (n=22) and 35.7% (n=94), respectively (Pearson chi-square; p=0.268).
output: Yes, researchers investigated the history of dental braces among participants. They found that 44% of individuals with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome wore dental braces, compared to 35.7% in the non-hypermobile group, though the difference between those specific groups wasn't statistically significant (p=0.268). However, a significant difference was noted when comparing hypermobile participants to those with a rigid Beighton score of 0/9.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. An obstetrician asks: 'What issues can arise in the first and second trimesters in women with joint hypermobility syndrome/hEDS?' Answer based on the article.
input: First trimester: No complications have been specifically reported as pertaining to the first trimester. Increased mucosal fragility can lead to spontaneous epistaxis and gingival bleeding predisposing to gingival inflammation and infections, caries and loss of teeth. Hypermobile EDS contributes to an increased tendency to joint subluxations, sprains, fasciitis and synovitis. The physiological changes in pregnancy can aggravate the joint symptoms. Gastro-intestinal involvement is common including delayed gastric emptying, sluggish bowel motility, reflux, gastritis, irritable bowel syndrome and constipation/diarrhoea. These can worsen in pregnancy. Some cases require PEG feeds for long-term nutritional support. Second trimester: It was thought that preterm labour was a well-recognized complication of pregnancies with JHS and this was commonly preceded by rupture of membranes; this is attributed to the fetus inheriting the condition, the fragility of fetal tissues manifested in chorionic membranes leading to premature ROM. More recent data do not support this association.
output:
First trimester:
- No complications are specifically reported.
- Mucosal fragility can cause nosebleeds and gingival bleeding, which predispose to gum inflammation, caries and tooth loss. Arrange dental review.
- Joint subluxations, sprains, fasciitis and synovitis may worsen with the physiological changes of pregnancy.
- GI problems (delayed gastric emptying, slow bowel motility, reflux, gastritis, IBS, constipation or diarrhea) are common and may worsen. A few patients need PEG feeding.

Second trimester:
- Preterm labor after premature rupture of membranes was once considered typical, attributed to fragile fetal membranes in an affected fetus. More recent data do not support this association.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. An obstetrician asks: 'What intrapartum and postpartum issues should I anticipate in women with JHS/hEDS?' Answer based on the article.
input: Women with JHS may experience quick or precipitate labour with an increased risk of perineal lacerations due to increased tissue fragility. Difficult forceps delivery should be avoided where possible. Traumatic and atonic postpartum haemorrhage can result from increased capillary fragility and defective connective tissue. No coagulation abnormalities have been reported in JHS. Delayed wound healing and atrophic scars are not uncommon. This has implications in pregnancy including healing of perineal or caesarean wounds. Increased tissue and capillary fragility can cause easy bruising and haematomas and can potentially make surgery difficult, therefore gentle tissue handling during surgery in these women is advised. Widespread musculoskeletal pain and muscle weaknesses cause excessive fatigue during pregnancy. These symptoms revert to pre-pregnancy state in the postnatal period.
output:
Issues to anticipate:
- Labor may be quick or precipitate, with a higher risk of perineal laceration because of tissue fragility. Avoid difficult forceps deliveries where possible.
- Postpartum hemorrhage (traumatic or atonic) can occur because of capillary and connective tissue fragility. No coagulation abnormality has been reported in JHS.
- Wound healing may be delayed, with atrophic scars, dehiscence or incisional hernia. Handle tissues gently in surgery, because bruising and hematomas are common.
- Joint problems require physiotherapy input and care with positioning in labor.
- Musculoskeletal pain and fatigue may be marked during pregnancy but usually return to baseline postnatally.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'How should anxiety, depression and neurodivergence be managed in patients with hEDS?' Answer based on the article.
input: Neurobehavioral/psychiatric manifestations. Validation of symptoms can be immensely helpful, as many with hEDS have been accused by health care professionals of malingering or diagnosed with primary psychiatric disorders. Establishing trust, rapport, and a supportive relationship with the affected individual is important. Anxiety and depression are a common result of the many morbidities a person with hEDS may experience. Psychological and/or symptom-oriented counseling can improve adaptation to and acceptance of these issues and their impact on quality of life. Cognitive behavioral therapy can be beneficial but requires active participation. Antidepressants may also be of benefit.

instruction: You are a medical educator. Based on the review, what explanations have been suggested for why hEDS is diagnosed more often in women?
input: There is an unexpected female predominance in hEDS despite suspected autosomal dominant inheritance. It is possible that women may be more frequently diagnosed due to a higher severity of symptoms than men. This may be explained by muscle mass and ligament stiffness being controlled by sex and leading to greater joint stability in men, as it is already known that women are more flexible than men. Additionally, women are also known to engage the medical system earlier than males. Understanding the protective factors that lead to reduced penetrance in men may be a key component of treating hEDS.
output: Even though hEDS is thought to be inherited equally by both sexes, many more women are diagnosed. Possible reasons include: women may simply have more severe symptoms; men generally have more muscle mass and stiffer ligaments, which may give their joints more stability, while women are naturally more flexible; and women tend to seek medical care earlier than men. Researchers think that understanding what protects men could help in finding treatments for hEDS.

instruction: A patient asks: 'I was told years ago that I have joint hypermobility syndrome. Now doctors talk about hEDS. Is this a different disease?' Answer based on the article.
input: The clinical spectrum of JHS is often clinically indistinguishable from hEDS according to an international panel of experts. Castori et al. demonstrated the evolving natural history by studying multi-generational pedigrees and concluded that both disorders may co-exist in the same pedigrees and could not be distinguished in the familial cases. It is, therefore, the consensus of the authors on behalf of the International Consortium on the Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes that the two conditions are part of the same clinical spectrum ranging from apparently symptomatic GJH to the most disabled individuals fitting the new diagnostic criteria for hEDS.
output: Not really a different disease. Experts found that joint hypermobility syndrome (JHS) and hypermobile EDS look practically the same in clinic, and both labels were often found in members of the same family. Because of this, the International Consortium on the Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes now sees them as parts of one spectrum—from people with symptomatic flexible joints at one end to people who are more severely affected and meet the stricter hEDS criteria at the other. What changed is mainly the name and the diagnostic rules, not your underlying condition. Your doctor can tell you where on that spectrum your symptoms fit today.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A family physician asks: 'Which presenting features should make me suspect hypermobile EDS in an adult patient?' Answer based on the article.
input: Common Presenting Features of Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome. History (features may occur sequentially): clumsiness, motor or speech delay in childhood, particularly with family history of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome; extreme flexibility or double-jointed—older adults may recall being double-jointed or extremely flexible in childhood; recurrent or chronic joint pains, may be limited or widespread; joint subluxation or dislocations without significant trauma—shoulder, knee, and hip most commonly affected; recurrent hernias, pelvic organ prolapse, or rectal prolapse, especially when no other known predisposing condition present. Physical findings: marfanoid habitus, may be present in up to one-third of patients; unusually soft, silky, or velvety skin; mildly hyperextensible skin (>1.5 cm on midvolar forearm of nondominant arm); mild scar atrophy; striae distensae or rubrae appearing in adolescence unassociated with weight gain or pregnancy; piezogenic papules at lateral heels. The strongest systemic findings associated with hypermobile EDS include anxiety disorders, chronic pain, fatigue, orthostatic intolerance, functional gastrointestinal disorders, and pelvic and bladder dysfunction. A U.K. patient survey found the median time to diagnosis was 10 years.
output:
Consider hEDS when you see a combination of the following.

History: childhood clumsiness or motor/speech delay (especially with a family history of EDS); extreme flexibility or being 'double-jointed', which older adults may only recall from childhood; recurrent or chronic joint pain, localized or widespread; subluxations or dislocations without significant trauma, most often shoulder, knee and hip; recurrent hernias or pelvic organ or rectal prolapse without another predisposing cause.

Examination: soft, velvety skin; mild skin hyperextensibility (>1.5 cm at the mid-volar forearm of the nondominant arm); mildly atrophic scars; striae appearing in adolescence without weight change or pregnancy; piezogenic heel papules; marfanoid habitus, present in up to one-third of patients.

Systemic clues: anxiety, chronic pain, fatigue, orthostatic intolerance, functional GI disorders, and pelvic or bladder dysfunction are the strongest associations.

These features often appear sequentially over years, which partly explains why the median time to diagnosis is about 10 years. Asking directly about childhood flexibility and prior dislocations is a high-yield first step.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'What is the typical pain phenotype in hEDS, and how should it guide treatment selection?' Answer based on the study.
input: According to the Margolis Pain Diagram, EDS-HT patients experienced pain on an average of 31% (+/-17.8) of their body surface, compared to 1% (+/-2.4) in the control subjects. Furthermore, approximately 40% of the patients presented with a nociceptive pain pattern, whereas in about 50% a predominantly neuropathic pain component was likely present.
output:
On the Margolis pain diagram, patients reported pain over an average of 31% of their body surface, compared with 1% in controls. About 40% had a predominantly nociceptive pattern and about 50% had a likely predominant neuropathic component.

Several pain mechanisms therefore coexist. In practice:
- Screen each patient for neuropathic features with a validated tool.
- Treat nociceptive (joint and muscle) and neuropathic components with appropriate, different strategies.
- Expect widespread pain rather than pain confined to one joint.

instruction: A patient asks: 'My echocardiogram showed a slightly widened aortic root. How often should it be checked?' Answer based on the article.
input: Echocardiography: In those with aortic root dilatation on initial echocardiogram: follow-up echocardiogram 1 yr after initial echocardiogram & if no change, follow-up echocardiogram in 5 yrs. In those with progressive aortic dilatation: continue annual echocardiography; if progressive dilatation stops, then echocardiogram every 3 yrs. Other vascular concerns, including significant aortic root dilatation, require referral to a cardiovascular specialist. Rapid aortic root growth, an indication for intervention, is defined as ≥0.5 cm in one year. Pregnant women with known aortic root dilatation should have an echocardiogram in each trimester. Echocardiography is not needed if the aortic root is normal prior to pregnancy.
output: According to the article, a repeat echocardiogram is usually done one year after the first one. If nothing has changed, the next check can be in five years. If the aortic root keeps widening, scans continue every year, and if the widening then stops, every three years. Significant widening needs a cardiovascular specialist, and growth of 0.5 cm or more in a single year is considered rapid and a reason to consider intervention. If you become pregnant, an echocardiogram is recommended in each trimester. Remember that in most people with hEDS this widening is mild, so follow the plan your cardiologist sets for you.

instruction: A woman with hEDS asks: 'I'm planning a pregnancy. What should I discuss with my doctors?' Answer based on the article.
input: Management of women with hEDS should include preconception assessment (e.g., musculoskeletal health and medication use), antenatal evaluation (e.g., joint instability, pelvic strength, hernias, and pain management), intrapartum planning (e.g., birth choices, mobility in labor, anesthesia), and postpartum care (e.g., wound healing, pelvic health, newborn/infant care). Musculoskeletal complications of hEDS including pain and joint instability may arise for the first time or worsen during pregnancy. In women with hEDS there is a higher incidence of preeclampsia, preterm rupture of membranes, preterm birth, antepartum hemorrhage, postpartum hemorrhage, hyperemesis gravidarum, caesarean wound infection, postpartum psychosis, post-traumatic stress disorder, precipitous labor, and delivery prior to arrival at planned place of birth.
output: Good planning helps. The article suggests discussing four stages: before conception—your joint health and which medications are safe in pregnancy; during pregnancy—joint instability, pelvic strength, hernias and pain management; for the birth—your birth options, staying mobile in labor and anesthesia (mention if local anesthetics have worked poorly for you); and after the birth—wound healing, pelvic floor recovery and practical help with caring for a newborn. Pain and joint instability can start or worsen during pregnancy. Some complications have been reported more often in women with hEDS, including pre-eclampsia, waters breaking early, preterm birth, heavy bleeding, severe pregnancy sickness, very fast labor (sometimes before reaching the hospital) and postnatal mental health problems, so it's wise to be followed by a team that knows about your hEDS and to plan your journey to the hospital in advance.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'My hEDS patient describes burning and tingling, but MRI and nerve conduction studies are normal. What should I consider?' Answer based on the article.
input: Nociceptive pain directly related to affected muscles, joints, and connective tissue is frequent. Neuropathic pain, characterized by allodynia and/or typical quality descriptors, such as electrical, burning, numb, or tingling, is also common. Anatomic imaging and functional electrodiagnostic studies are often negative even in the face of subjective symptoms highly suggestive of a neuropathic etiology. Skin biopsy may reveal reduction of intradermal nerve fiber density, suggestive of small fiber neuropathy. Some potential etiologies of pain include spasm of muscles, tendons, and other connective tissue; direct trauma due to joint instability; and nerve entrapment. Osteoarthritis, secondary to joint instability, is also a likely factor. Central sensitization, generalized hyperalgesia, and similar mechanisms may contribute in later stages.

instruction: A patient with hEDS says: 'Nothing seems to work for my fatigue, and I'm thinking of trying an expensive treatment I found online.' Respond based on the article.
input: Clinicians and patients should remain aware that some patients do not show meaningful responses to therapy. Patients with intractable, chronic and disabling conditions are prone to feelings of abandonment and may be vulnerable to potentially toxic therapies or exploitative practitioners. For such patients, the long-term supportive and protective role of the physician can be invaluable. Treatment algorithms for fatigue are poorly defined and therapy is frequently ineffective and so aims of treatment should be realistic. Treatment should focus on improving symptoms, maintaining function and providing social, physical and nutritional support.
output: It's completely understandable to look for anything that might help when you're exhausted and treatments haven't worked. The article honestly acknowledges that some people don't respond well to therapy, and that this can lead to feeling abandoned—and makes people vulnerable to potentially harmful treatments or practitioners who exploit them. Before spending money on something, it's worth discussing it with a doctor you trust; a long-term, supportive relationship with a physician can protect you. Realistic goals also help: the aim is to improve symptoms, maintain what you can do and get social, physical and nutritional support, rather than a single cure.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'What are the five Beighton manoeuvres and how is the score calculated?' Answer based on the text.
input: Beighton Scoring: For the Beighton scoring, the following items were evaluated; 1) Placement of hands flat on the floor without bending the knees, 2) Hyperextension of the elbow to >=10 degrees, 3) Hyperextension of the knee to >=10 degrees, 4) Opposition of the thumb to the volar aspect of the ipsilateral forearm, and 5) Passive dorsiflexion of the fifth metacarpophalangeal joint to >=90 degrees.
output:
The Beighton score has five manoeuvres, scored out of 9 points:
1. Palms flat on the floor with knees straight: 1 point.
2. Elbow hyperextension of 10° or more: 1 point per side.
3. Knee hyperextension of 10° or more: 1 point per side.
4. Thumb apposition to the volar forearm: 1 point per side.
5. Passive dorsiflexion of the fifth MCP joint to 90° or more: 1 point per side.

Four manoeuvres are bilateral (2 points each) and the forward bend is a single point. Interpret the total using age-appropriate cut-offs, and remember that the score samples only a few joints.

instruction: A patient asks: 'My geneticist ordered genetic tests even though there's no gene for hEDS. Why?' Answer as a health educator based on the study.
input: Among 907 patients referred for suspected hEDS, 178 met the 2017 diagnostic criteria for hEDS. Genetic testing identified an alternative or additional diagnosis in 47 of these individuals (26.4%), with clinical implications requiring distinct management strategies. The primary use of genetic testing in hEDS evaluation is to exclude alternative diagnoses. Generalized joint hypermobility is a shared feature in many inherited disorders, and multisystem manifestations of hEDS are usually non-specific and shared across many genetic and multifactorial disorders.
output: It's a good sign that your geneticist is being thorough. There's still no test that confirms hEDS, but flexible joints and many hEDS symptoms also occur in other inherited conditions. Part of diagnosing hEDS is ruling those out, and genetic tests help with that. In one large clinic, about 1 in 4 people (26.4%) who clinically met the hEDS criteria turned out to have a different or additional condition on genetic testing, and in each case it changed their care. A negative result doesn't rule out hEDS. It means other explanations have been checked.

instruction: You are a health educator explaining pain in hEDS. Based on the article, what kinds of pain can people with hEDS have, and why can tests come back normal?
input: Nociceptive pain directly related to affected muscles, joints, and connective tissue is frequent. Neuropathic pain, characterized by allodynia and/or typical quality descriptors, such as electrical, burning, numb, or tingling, is also common. Anatomic imaging and functional electrodiagnostic studies are often negative even in the face of subjective symptoms highly suggestive of a neuropathic etiology. Skin biopsy may reveal reduction of intradermal nerve fiber density, suggestive of small fiber neuropathy. Some potential etiologies of pain include spasm of muscles, tendons, and other connective tissue; direct trauma due to joint instability; and nerve entrapment. Osteoarthritis, secondary to joint instability, is also a likely factor. Central sensitization, generalized hyperalgesia, and similar mechanisms may contribute in later stages.
output: People with hEDS often have more than one kind of pain at the same time. Nociceptive pain comes directly from muscles, joints and connective tissue—for example from muscle spasms, injuries caused by unstable joints, or arthritis that develops after years of joint instability. Neuropathic (nerve) pain is also common and is often described as electric, burning, numb or tingling; sometimes even a light touch hurts (allodynia). It can come from trapped nerves or from damage to tiny nerve fibers in the skin (small fiber neuropathy), which a skin biopsy may show. Scans and nerve conduction tests are often normal even when nerve pain is clearly present, because they don't detect these small fibers well. Over time, the nervous system itself can become more sensitive to pain (central sensitization).

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'Is there evidence of immune involvement in hEDS?' Answer based on the research.
input: Source 1: Proteomic analysis of serum from female hEDS patients and matched controls revealed 35 differentially expressed proteins, with 43% involved in the complement cascade and 80% linked to immune, coagulation, or inflammatory pathways. Our findings indicate a systemic immune dysregulation, particularly involving the complement system and profibrotic cytokines, as a common feature in hEDS pathophysiology. These findings challenge the traditional view of hEDS as solely a connective tissue disorder. Source 2: KLK15, a secreted serine protease, is expressed in connective and immune tissues. A KLK15 knock-in mouse model recapitulated hEDS features in tendons and cardiac valves and exhibited dysregulated cytokine profiles. This study reframes hEDS as a condition involving matrix remodeling and immune signaling beyond collagen defects.
output:
Emerging evidence suggests there is:
- Serum proteomics found 35 differentially expressed proteins in women with hEDS. 43% were in the complement cascade and 80% were linked to immune, coagulation or inflammatory pathways. Profibrotic cytokines were also altered.
- A KLK15 variant found in hEDS families produced tendon and heart-valve changes in knock-in mice, along with dysregulated cytokine profiles. KLK15 is expressed in connective and immune tissues.

The authors propose reframing hEDS as involving matrix remodeling and immune signaling, not only collagen structure. This is research-level evidence and does not yet change clinical management.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'Should I restrict sports or prohibit joint hyperextension in patients with hEDS?' Answer based on the article.
input: High-impact activity may increase the risk for acute subluxation/dislocation and acute and chronic pain. Some sports, such as tackle football, may not be suitable but should be discussed on an individual basis. Most sports and activities are acceptable with appropriate precautions. Joint hyperextension may not need to be avoided. In a randomized controlled trial of physical therapy among 26 children and adolescents with joint hypermobility and knee pain, those allowed to exercise into hyperextension had similar improvement in pain score and better improvement in psychosocial score compared to those restricted to neutral joint position.
output:
Generally, no.
- Most sports and activities are acceptable with appropriate precautions. High-impact activity may increase the risk of subluxation or dislocation and of pain, and some sports, such as tackle football, may be unsuitable. Decide individually.
- Hyperextension may not need to be avoided. In an RCT of 26 children and adolescents with hypermobility and knee pain, those allowed to exercise into hyperextension had similar improvement in pain and greater improvement in psychosocial scores than those restricted to a neutral position.
