instruction: A patient with hEDS and POTS asks: 'What can help my dizziness and racing heart when I stand up?' Answer based on the article.
input: Cardiovascular. Standard treatments for neurally mediated hypotension and postural orthostatic tachycardia are advised, including avoidance of sudden postural change, consideration of lower extremity and/or abdominal compression garments, exercise to increase muscle strength and improve tone, supplementation of sodium and water to expand the blood volume, and sometimes pharmacologic treatment with beta-blockers, midodrine, fludrocortisone, ivabradine, and/or other medications initiated by a clinician experienced in autonomic medicine. Commercially available electrolyte tablets can facilitate oral expansion of blood volume.
output: The article describes standard measures for POTS and low blood pressure on standing: avoid getting up suddenly (move from lying to sitting to standing in stages); consider compression garments for the legs and/or abdomen; do exercises that build muscle strength and tone, especially in the legs; and increase salt and fluid intake to raise blood volume—electrolyte tablets can make this easier. Some people also need medication, such as beta-blockers, midodrine, fludrocortisone or ivabradine, started by a clinician experienced in autonomic disorders. Please check with your doctor before increasing salt, especially if you have high blood pressure or kidney or heart problems.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'Why is fascia being proposed as a unifying framework for hEDS/HSD?' Answer based on the review.
input: Fascia is not merely a structural support matrix—it is a highly dynamic, innervated, and vascularized connective tissue network involved in force transmission, proprioception, pain modulation, and intercellular communication. The multilayered nature of fascia—including superficial, deep, visceral, and neural components—offers a plausible anatomical basis for the systemic manifestations observed in disorders such as hEDS and HSD. Fascia is not a passive structural element but an active tissue involved in mechanosensation, immune modulation, force transmission, and fluid balance.
output:
Fascia is not merely a structural support. It is a dynamic, innervated, vascularized connective tissue network involved in force transmission, proprioception, pain modulation, intercellular communication, immune modulation and fluid balance. Its multilayered organization (superficial, deep, visceral and neural) offers a plausible anatomical basis for the systemic manifestations of hEDS and HSD.

This framework is still emerging. It is a model for research, not yet a basis for diagnosis or specific treatment.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'Why should fatigue be specifically assessed in patients with hEDS?' Answer based on the article.
input: Fatigue is one of the most common complaints among those with hEDS. Chronic fatigue in hEDS includes bodily and mental fatigue which only minimally improves with rest and often fits well into the diagnostic criteria of CFS. The fatigue in hEDS, as in the general population, is under recognized and may increase in prevalence with age. Like in the general population, fatigue in hEDS is multifactorial with contributing factors including pain, sleep disturbance, dysautonomia, medications, and/or allergies. It has been associated with greater pain, functional impairment, and psychological distress as well as decreased QoL.
output:
Fatigue is one of the most common complaints in hEDS, yet it is under-recognized and may become more prevalent with age. It is both physical and mental, improves little with rest, and often fits the criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome.

It is multifactorial. Contributors include pain, sleep disturbance, dysautonomia, medications and allergies.

Fatigue is associated with more pain, functional impairment and psychological distress, and with lower quality of life. Ask about it explicitly and look for treatable contributors.

instruction: A patient asks: 'Is there a genetic test for hEDS?' Answer as a medical educator based on the article.
input: hEDS, for the most part, is inherited as an autosomal dominant disorder of connective tissue but other patterns of inheritance can be seen in some families; however, this may be confounded by non-penetrance, sex-influence as well as genetic heterogeneity. Unfortunately, unlike the other types of EDS, hEDS has no known genetic etiology responsible for any significant portion of this population. JH itself is multifactorial with age, gender, weight, training, and other aspects that influence this phenotype. Twin studies have determined that the concordance of JH among dizygotic twins was 36% in 472 female twin pairs, whereas monozygotic twins had a concordance rate of 60% in 483 female twin pairs suggesting a strong genetic trait with multifactorial influences.
output: Not at the moment. Unlike the other types of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, no gene has been found that explains hEDS in a meaningful number of patients, so the diagnosis is made by a clinical examination and your medical and family history. hEDS usually runs in families in an autosomal dominant way (one affected parent can pass it on), but the pattern can be blurred because not everyone who carries it shows symptoms, and sex plays a role. Twin studies support a strong genetic component: identical twins share joint hypermobility in about 60% of cases versus 36% in non-identical twins. Joint flexibility is also affected by age, sex, weight and training.

instruction: You are a medical educator. Based on the review, what is generalized hypermobility spectrum disorder (G-HSD), and how can different family members be affected?
input: The HT-EDS phenotype significantly overlaps and is now thought to be clinically indistinguishable from joint hypermobility syndrome (JHS) and benign joint hypermobility syndrome (BJHS). In order to resolve this conundrum, a continuous spectrum of hypermobility was proposed. Patients who present with some mandatory features included in the hEDS criteria and those diagnosed with these phenotypically similar disorders can be classified as having 'Generalised Hypermobility Spectrum Disorder' (G-HSD), one of the 'Hypermobility Spectrum Disorders' (HSD) which reside in the middle of the spectrum. Individuals within the same pedigree may show different hypermobility phenotypes described in the spectrum.
output: Generalized hypermobility spectrum disorder (G-HSD) describes people who have hypermobility in many joints and some of the features of hEDS, but not enough to meet all the hEDS criteria. It sits in the middle of a continuous hypermobility spectrum, between harmless flexible joints at one end and hEDS at the other. Many people previously diagnosed with joint hypermobility syndrome now fall into this category. Interestingly, members of the same family can sit at different points on this spectrum—one may have hEDS, another G-HSD, and another only flexible joints without symptoms.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'What advice should I give about daytime napping in patients with hEDS-related fatigue?' Answer based on the article.
input: While daytime napping may be beneficial as part of rest and relaxation, it may in some cases lead to either a shift or reversal of the day-night sleep cycle, with resultant difficulty sleeping at night and daytime somnolence, and therefore be more detrimental than beneficial.
output:
Daytime napping can be useful as part of rest and relaxation. However, in some patients it shifts or even reverses the day-night sleep cycle, leading to night-time insomnia and daytime sleepiness, and then does more harm than good.

Ask about naps when assessing sleep. If night sleep is disrupted, consider limiting naps.

instruction: A patient asks: 'Should I worry about my heart if I have hEDS?' Answer as a medical educator based on the article.
input: Mild dilation of the aortic root may develop in up to one-third of children or young adults, but is unlikely to progress and typically does not require any specific treatment. Baseline echocardiography is not recommended based on these findings alone but depend on other symptoms and differential diagnoses upon presentation. Mitral valve prolapse (MVP) was previously considered a common feature of EDS, but that was prior to the establishment of more rigorous criteria for the diagnosis of MVP. Since then, some studies show no increase in the frequency of clinically significant MVP and others show an MVP frequency of 28-67% among hEDS patients. It is reasonable to still consider MVP as a potential clue for hEDS, but the true clinical significance is not yet known.
output: In general, serious heart problems are not typical of hEDS. Up to one-third of children and young adults with hEDS may have a slightly widened aortic root (the start of the main artery leaving the heart), but it usually does not get worse and typically needs no treatment. Mitral valve prolapse, where a heart valve bulges slightly, was once thought to be very common in EDS, but studies using stricter definitions disagree—some find no increase, others find it in 28-67% of people with hEDS. A routine heart ultrasound (echocardiogram) is not automatically recommended just because you have hEDS; your doctor will decide based on your symptoms and examination. If you have chest symptoms, fainting or a family history of heart disease, tell your doctor.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'What kinds of alternative or coexisting diagnoses have been found by genetic testing in patients who met the hEDS criteria?' Answer based on the study.
input: Out of a total of 907 patients referred for suspected hEDS, 178 individuals (19.62%) fulfilled the diagnostic criteria based on clinical evaluation. Among those, 47 individuals (26.4%) were found to have additional or alternative diagnoses. 6 individuals had positive results in genes associated with HCTDs and skeletal disorders (Loeys-Dietz syndrome type 3, Larsen syndrome, cutis laxa, adult-onset hypophosphatasia, multiple epiphyseal dysplasia). 11 individuals had positive results in genes associated with neuromuscular disorders (myotonia congenita, collagen VI-related myopathy, slow-channel congenital myasthenic syndrome, limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, POLG-related spectrum disorder, oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy, spinocerebellar ataxia types 8 and 10). 7 individuals had chromosomal abnormality or CNVs (16p11.2 duplication, 16p13.11 microduplication, 15q13.3 deletion, 1q21.1 deletion, mosaic Turner syndrome, triple X syndrome). 22 individuals had positive results in genes associated with disorders of immune system (common variable immunodeficiency, familial Mediterranean fever, APS1, porphyria variegata); of this group, 12 individuals had extra copies of TPSAB1 and elevated tryptase levels (hereditary alpha tryptasemia). One individual had hemochromatosis type 1. The results suggest that hypermobility may present a shared phenotype across a spectrum of disorders, including inflammatory diseases, monogenic syndromes, and chromosomal abnormalities.
output:
Of the 47 patients (26.4% of those meeting the criteria) with a positive result, findings fell into four broad groups:

- Heritable connective tissue and skeletal disorders (6): Loeys-Dietz syndrome type 3, Larsen syndrome, cutis laxa, adult-onset hypophosphatasia, multiple epiphyseal dysplasia.
- Neuromuscular disorders (11): myotonia congenita, collagen VI-related myopathy, slow-channel congenital myasthenic syndrome, limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, POLG-related disorders, oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy, spinocerebellar ataxias 8 and 10.
- Chromosomal abnormalities and CNVs (7): 16p11.2 duplication, 16p13.11 microduplication, 15q13.3 deletion, 1q21.1 deletion, mosaic Turner syndrome, triple X.
- Immune and other disorders (22): common variable immunodeficiency, familial Mediterranean fever, APS1, porphyria variegata. Twelve of these had hereditary alpha-tryptasemia (extra TPSAB1 copies). One additional patient had hemochromatosis.

Several of these, such as Loeys-Dietz syndrome or CVID, carry serious implications for surveillance or treatment. The authors conclude that hypermobility can be a shared phenotype across inflammatory, monogenic and chromosomal disorders, so a clinical hEDS diagnosis should not end the search when atypical features are present.

instruction: You are a medical educator explaining chronic pain research in EDS. Based on the abstract, what were the specific aims of the study regarding pain modulation and the nature of pain in EDS-HT patients?
input: Purpose: ...Therefore, this study aims to assess the nature of pain (nociceptive / neuropathic / dysfunctional pain) and the endogenous pain modulation in EDS-HT.
output: The study aimed to evaluate the exact nature of pain—specifically distinguishing between nociceptive, neuropathic, and dysfunctional pain—while also assessing endogenous pain modulation in patients with the hypermobility type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS-HT).

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'How should I structure shared decision-making for a patient with hEDS and significant fatigue?' Answer based on the article.
input: To facilitate effective management the clinician needs to establish a collaborative relationship with the patient and their carers. Engagement with the family is particularly important for children and young people, and for people with severe fatigue. The patient and their clinician should share decision making. Together this might include: understanding the need to exclude underlying diseases and disorders; recognizing the reality and impact (physical, emotional, social [including education and employment]) of the condition and the symptoms; setting realistic goals and timelines for improvement, being prepared to manage set-backs/relapses; exploring the range of interventions available, taking account of the patients' age, the severity of their symptoms, their preferences and experiences, and the outcome of previous treatment. People with severe fatigue may need support from a multidisciplinary team, coordinated by a named healthcare professional, usually their general practitioner.

instruction: You are a health educator discussing chronic pain patterns. Based on the abstract, what types of pain do patients with EDS-HT experience and how much of their body surface is affected?
input: According to the Margolis Pain Diagram, EDS-HT patients experienced pain on an average of 31% (+/-17.8) of their body surface, compared to 1% (+/-2.4) in the control subjects. Furthermore, approximately 40% of the patients presented with a nociceptive pain pattern, whereas in about 50% a predominantly neuropathic pain component was likely present.
output: According to the findings, EDS-HT patients experienced pain across an average of 31% of their total body surface, compared to just 1% in healthy controls. Furthermore, analysis showed that about 40% of these patients presented with a nociceptive pain pattern, while roughly 50% likely experienced a predominantly neuropathic pain component, indicating that multiple coexisting pain mechanisms are at play.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'Why is hEDS diagnosed predominantly in women if inheritance is autosomal dominant?' Answer based on the review.
input: There is an unexpected female predominance in hEDS despite suspected autosomal dominant inheritance. It is possible that women may be more frequently diagnosed due to a higher severity of symptoms than men. This may be explained by muscle mass and ligament stiffness being controlled by sex and leading to greater joint stability in men, as it is already known that women are more flexible than men. Additionally, women are also known to engage the medical system earlier than males. Understanding the protective factors that lead to reduced penetrance in men may be a key component of treating hEDS.
output:
The proposed explanations are:
- Women may have more severe symptoms and so are diagnosed more often.
- Sex-related differences in muscle mass and ligament stiffness may give men greater joint stability, and women are known to be more flexible.
- Women tend to engage with the medical system earlier than men.

The authors suggest that understanding the protective factors behind reduced penetrance in men could inform treatment. Clinically, do not dismiss the diagnosis in men.

instruction: A patient says: 'I'm tired of being sent from one specialist to another who only looks at one joint.' Respond based on the article.
input: Specialties continue to operate in isolated 'silos', separated according to discipline, body system, or function. Conditions with multisystemic impact add clinical complexity to primary care encounters and frequently lead to referrals to multiple specialists. As a result, patients feel that their clinical care is fragmented and focused on individual body parts rather than their illness as a whole. According to one participant they have a sort of, 'you're here for one joint' approach, which is quite difficult, because you go: 'Well, I'm floopy all over'. Participants expressed the need for a more patient-centered, holistic approach to complex, multisystemic conditions like hEDS/HSD.
output: That frustration is very understandable, and research shows it's widely shared. Healthcare is often organized in 'silos', with each specialty looking at one body part or system. hEDS/HSD affects many systems at once, so people end up with many referrals and care that feels fragmented—one participant described being treated as if they were 'here for one joint' when they were 'floopy all over'. Patients in these studies called for a holistic approach. In practice, it can help to have one coordinating clinician, often your family doctor, who keeps the whole picture in mind and connects the different specialists.

instruction: You are a medical educator explaining scientific findings to the public. Based on the article, explain what 'generalized joint hypermobility' means and how common it is in young adults.
input: Results: In total, 77.3% (n=259) of participants had any class of joint hypermobility and 25.9% (n=87) of them had generalized class. Generalized joint hypermobility was defined in participants firstly as a Beighton scoring of >=4/9... and secondly with Beighton scoring >=5/9.
output: Generalized joint hypermobility means that a person has widespread joint flexibility affecting multiple areas—specifically the upper limbs, lower limbs, and the spine (axial skeleton) all at once. In a study of healthy university students aged 18 to 25, researchers found that about 25.9% of young adults actually met the criteria for generalized joint hypermobility, showing it is far more common than many people realize.

instruction: A patient with hEDS asks: 'Should I be tested for POTS and mast cell activation syndrome just because I have hEDS?' Answer as a health educator based on the expert review.
input: Testing for POTS/MCAS should be targeted to patients presenting with clinical manifestations of POTS/MCAS, but universal testing for POTS/MCAS in all patients with hEDS/HSDs is not supported by the current evidence. Testing for mast cell disorders including MCAS should be considered in patients with hEDS/HSDs and DGBI who also present with episodic symptoms that suggest a more generalized mast cell disorder (eg, visceral and somatic pain, pruritus, flushing, sweating, urticaria, angioedema, wheezing, tachycardia, abdominal cramping, vomiting, nausea, diarrhea, urogynecological and neurological complaints) involving 2 or more physiological systems (eg, cutaneous, GI, cardiac, respiratory, and neuropsychiatric).
output:
Not automatically. Experts from the American Gastroenterological Association advise testing only when you actually have symptoms of these conditions, not for everyone with hEDS.

- POTS: worth checking if you get symptoms when upright, such as a racing heart, dizziness or feeling faint.
- MCAS: worth checking if you have episodes of symptoms affecting two or more body systems at once. Examples are flushing, itching, hives or swelling (skin); cramping, nausea, vomiting or diarrhea (gut); a racing heart; or wheezing.

If this sounds like you, tell your doctor which symptoms you have and when they occur. A diary of flare-ups can help.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'What GI manifestations should I expect in hEDS, and what is a sensible initial workup?' Answer based on the article.
input: Collectively, functional features may be observed in 1/3 to 3/4 of the patients with an increasing rate by age. Manifestations variably include gastroesophageal reflux, heartburn, bloating, recurrent abdominal pain, irritable bowel syndrome, constipation, and diarrhea. Constipation with or without other features of voiding dysfunction is usually the earliest sign of gastrointestinal involvement. Standard investigations are usually carried out without severe complications in hEDS, but they often have negative or inconsistent results. Treatment of functional GI complaints in hEDS is problematic due to the absence of tailored strategies and an apparent resistance to pharmacologic treatments at standard dosages. The exclusion of common comorbidities, such as celiac disease, lactose intolerance, and Helicobacter pylori infection, is reasonable at first examination.
output:
Functional GI symptoms occur in one-third to three-quarters of patients and become more frequent with age. They include reflux and heartburn, bloating, recurrent abdominal pain, IBS, constipation and diarrhea. Constipation, sometimes with voiding dysfunction, is often the earliest GI sign.

Standard investigations are usually safe but often normal or inconsistent.

At the first assessment, it is reasonable to exclude:
- celiac disease;
- lactose intolerance;
- Helicobacter pylori.

Response to standard drug doses may be poor, and no hEDS-specific treatment strategies exist.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. An internist asks: 'What are the key differential diagnoses of joint hypermobility, and which features point away from hEDS?' Answer based on the article.
input: Selected Differential Diagnosis of Joint Hypermobility. Acquired conditions including diffuse degenerative disorders of muscles, joints, or nerves; hypothyroidism; or malnutrition: suggestive medical history. Chromosomal and genomic disorders including Down syndrome, aneuploidies (47,XXY; 47,XXX), and several microdeletion and microduplication syndromes: dysmorphic features, hypogonadism. Hereditary cutis laxa: loose, inelastic skin. Hereditary myopathies (Bethlem, Ullrich, and others): hypotonia and weakness, joint hyperlaxity and contractures. Loeys-Dietz syndrome: arterial tortuosity and aortic aneurysms, cleft palate/bifid uvula, hypertelorism, hypotonia. Marfan syndrome, Beals syndrome, MASS phenotype, and arterial tortuosity syndrome: ectopia lentis in Marfan syndrome, mitral valve prolapse in MASS phenotype, progressive ascending aortic dilation, tortuous medium and large arteries. Multiple congenital anomaly or intellectual disability disorders including RASopathies, Kabuki make-up syndrome, FG syndrome, fragile X syndrome. Other variants of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome including classical, vascular, and rarer forms: acrogeria, arterial, viscus, or lung rupture, muscle weakness, pronounced skin hyperextensibility, unusual skin fragility, papyraceous or hemosideric scars. Skeletal dysplasias (osteogenesis imperfecta type I, Larsen syndrome, Desbuquois syndrome): blue sclerae, bone fragility, neonatal joint dislocations. The presence of marfanoid features requires distinguishing between hypermobile EDS and Marfan-related syndromes.
output:
Features that should make you look beyond hEDS:

- Other EDS types: pronounced skin hyperextensibility, unusual skin fragility, papyraceous or hemosiderotic scars, acrogeria, or arterial, visceral or lung rupture. Vascular EDS is the critical diagnosis not to miss.
- Marfan and related aortopathies (Marfan, Beals, MASS, arterial tortuosity syndrome): ectopia lentis, progressive ascending aortic dilation, tortuous arteries. Marfanoid habitus alone is common in hEDS, so these signs are what distinguish the two.
- Loeys-Dietz syndrome: aortic aneurysm or arterial tortuosity, cleft palate or bifid uvula, hypertelorism.
- Hereditary myopathies (e.g., Bethlem, Ullrich): hypotonia and weakness, with joint laxity coexisting with contractures.
- Skeletal dysplasias (OI type I, Larsen, Desbuquois): blue sclerae, bone fragility, neonatal dislocations.
- Hereditary cutis laxa: loose, inelastic (rather than stretchy) skin.
- Chromosomal or genomic disorders and multiple-anomaly/intellectual-disability syndromes (e.g., aneuploidies, microdeletions/duplications, RASopathies, fragile X): dysmorphic features, hypogonadism, intellectual disability.
- Acquired causes: degenerative neuromuscular or joint disease, hypothyroidism, malnutrition.

When any of these features are present, targeted genetic testing or specialist referral is generally indicated before labelling the patient as hEDS.

instruction: You are a medical educator. Based on the article, explain why the 2017 diagnostic criteria for hEDS were made stricter than earlier criteria and what happens to people who no longer meet them.
input: The new criteria of hEDS are stricter than the old Villefranche nosology and the Brighton criteria. This is intended to define a more homogeneous phenotype shared among patients who require long-term medical attention for hEDS and to facilitate scientific identification of the underlying genetic cause(s) of the condition. Accordingly, some patients meeting the old Villefranche and Brighton criteria will not meet the new hEDS criteria. For all these individuals not showing a sufficiently convincing hEDS phenotype, some alternative labels within the above-mentioned spectrum are presented.
output: The 2017 criteria were made stricter for two main reasons: to describe a more uniform group of patients who need long-term care for hEDS, and to make it easier for scientists to find the gene or genes that cause it—research works best when everyone in a study group truly has the same condition. As a result, some people who were diagnosed under the older Villefranche or Brighton criteria may not meet the new hEDS criteria. That does not mean their symptoms are not real. They are given other labels within the same hypermobility spectrum, most often a hypermobility spectrum disorder (HSD).

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'How does symptomatic joint hypermobility usually present, and how does it relate to fibromyalgia?' Answer based on the article.
input: Adults may recall being flexible as a child, and being able to perform 'party tricks' with their joints. The two more common patterns of presentation are with: (1) a limited number of painful and/or unstable joints or (2) chronic widespread musculoskeletal pain (which may have been diagnosed as fibromyalgia). In the former group, the more common problematic or unstable joints often presenting with recurrent subluxations/dislocations or pain are the shoulder, knee, and ankle. It is important to recognize that there are many causes for both localized and widespread joint or musculoskeletal pain, and that the presence of pain alone without associated JH is insufficient to establish a diagnosis of EDS.
output:
There are two common presentations:
1. A few painful or unstable joints, typically the shoulder, knee or ankle, with recurrent subluxations or dislocations.
2. Chronic widespread musculoskeletal pain whose distribution and description can be virtually indistinguishable from fibromyalgia.

Ask about childhood flexibility and 'party tricks'. In patients labelled with fibromyalgia, examine for generalized joint hypermobility. Pain alone, without hypermobility, is insufficient for an EDS diagnosis, and other causes of localized or widespread pain must be considered.

instruction: You are a health educator. Based on the article, describe how hEDS can change over a person's lifetime.
input: In an Italian study on disease progression with 21 hEDS patients, the existence of three 'discrete' disease phases was proposed: a 'hypermobility' phase, a 'pain' phase, and a 'stiffness' phase. The 'hypermobility' phase dominates the first several years of life with contortionism and propensity for sprains and dislocations. The 'pain' phase is characterized by generalization and progressive chronicity of musculoskeletal pain, summation of other forms of chronic pain, such as pelvic pain and headache, as well as exacerbation of fatigue. This phase typically starts in the second to the fourth decade of life. A generalized reduction of joint mobility dominates the 'stiffness' phase. The three-step model can remain a prototypical description of the potential disease course, but not every patient experiences all three phases and the rate of transition between phases can be highly variable.
output: Researchers have described three possible phases of hEDS. (1) The hypermobility phase, in early childhood: children are very bendy and prone to sprains and dislocations, and pain is often limited to the legs ('growing pains') or to tasks like handwriting. (2) The pain phase, usually starting between the teens and the forties: pain becomes more widespread and long-lasting, other pain such as headaches or pelvic pain may appear, and fatigue gets worse. (3) The stiffness phase, seen in some adults and older people: joints become less mobile, and pain, fatigue, muscle weakness and earlier injuries can limit daily function. This is a typical picture, not a fixed path—not everyone goes through all three phases, and the pace varies a lot from person to person.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'When is tenascin-X deficiency relevant in a patient with an hEDS-like phenotype?' Answer based on the article.
input: A minority of cases have been reported to be due to a haploinsufficiency of tenascin X (TNXB). However, the haploinsufficiency was not penetrant in males and only partially in females (9 out of 14). TNXB lies near CYP21A2, the gene associated with congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH). Merke et al. reported in several CAH individuals, an hEDS-like phenotype due to chromosomal microdeletion and coined the syndrome CAH-X. Tenascin-X is an extracellular matrix protein and potentially can affect connective tissue in its various forms. However, the exact physiologic process remains unknown and heterozygous tenascin-X deficiency accounts for only a small percentage of hEDS.
output:
TNXB haploinsufficiency explains only a small minority of hEDS-like cases. Penetrance is incomplete: it was absent in males and present in only 9 of 14 females in the original report.

It is especially relevant in patients with congenital adrenal hyperplasia. TNXB lies next to CYP21A2, and contiguous microdeletions can cause CAH-X, which combines CAH with an hEDS-like phenotype.

In practice, consider TNXB in patients with CAH and hypermobility, and include it in connective tissue gene panels. Do not expect it to explain most hEDS presentations.

instruction: A newly diagnosed patient asks: 'I've just been diagnosed with hEDS. What check-ups should I have from now on?' Answer based on the article.
input: There are no specific surveillance guidelines for hEDS. Specific concerns should be followed up based on clinical need and standard protocols. Recommended surveillance: Musculoskeletal: assess for joint manifestations & current degree of pain & disability, annually or at each visit. DXA scan in those with height loss >1 inch, atypical/low trauma fractures, or radiographs suggestive of osteopenia. Annually or at each visit assess: bleeding issues; functional bowel disorders; autonomic dysfunction; orthodontia needs & periodontal disease; phonation & respiratory issues; sleep issues; xerophthalmia, refractive errors & diplopia; headaches, cord & nerve root pathology, dystonia & peripheral neuropathy; soft tissue inflammation, co-occurring rheumatologic disorders & mast cell activation disorders; psychosocial assessment for depression, anxiety, affective disorder, autism & ADHD; interstitial cystitis, urinary incontinence, pelvic organ prolapse, dysmenorrhea, menorrhagia & dyspareunia.
output: There's no single official follow-up schedule for hEDS; check-ups are based on your needs. The article suggests reviewing these areas once a year or at each visit: joints, pain and how much they limit you; bleeding or bruising; bowel problems; dizziness or other autonomic symptoms; teeth, gums and orthodontic needs; voice, breathing and sleep; eyes (dryness, vision changes, double vision); headaches and nerve symptoms; inflammation, other rheumatic conditions and mast cell symptoms; mood, anxiety and neurodevelopmental conditions such as autism or ADHD; and bladder, pelvic floor and menstrual or sexual pain. A bone density scan (DXA) is suggested only if you lose more than an inch of height, break a bone with little trauma, or X-rays suggest thin bones. A yearly review with your family doctor is a good place to go through this list.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A gynecologist asks: 'Which gynecologic complaints are common in women with hEDS?' Answer based on the article.
input: Gynecologic complaints from patients with hEDS are commonly encountered. In a study with 223 women with EDS, 67% self-reported mucosal problems with their genital area. Heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia) was reported by 26–76% of hEDS females. Painful intercourse was also reported by 30–57% of women with EDS and hEDS.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'Should every patient with suspected hEDS have an echocardiogram?' Summarize what the sources say, including any differences between them.
input: Source 1 (American Family Physician review, 2021): Screening echocardiography should be performed to evaluate for aortic root dilation or mitral valve prolapse in patients with possible hypermobile EDS. Source 2 (Tinkle et al., 2017): Mild dilation of the aortic root may develop in up to one-third of children or young adults, but is unlikely to progress and typically does not require any specific treatment. Baseline echocardiography is not recommended based on these findings alone but depend on other symptoms and differential diagnoses upon presentation. Source 3 (GeneReviews, 2024): In those with aortic root dilatation on initial echocardiogram: follow-up echocardiogram 1 yr after initial echocardiogram & if no change, follow-up echocardiogram in 5 yrs. In those with progressive aortic dilatation: continue annual echocardiography. Rapid aortic root growth, an indication for intervention, is defined as ≥0.5 cm in one year.
output:
The sources differ.

- The 2021 American Family Physician review recommends screening echocardiography in patients with possible hEDS, to look for aortic root dilation and MVP. MVP and aortic root dilation also count toward Feature A of the 2017 criteria.
- Tinkle et al. (2017, International Consortium) note that mild aortic root dilation occurs in up to one-third of children and young adults with hEDS but rarely progresses. They do not recommend baseline echo on that basis alone, and instead let symptoms and the differential diagnosis guide it.

In practice, echocardiography is clearly indicated when there are cardiac symptoms, a murmur, a family history of aortic disease or sudden death, or features suggesting Marfan, Loeys-Dietz or vascular EDS. Many clinicians also obtain one during the diagnostic evaluation.

If dilation is found, GeneReviews suggests:
- repeat echo at 1 year, then at 5 years if stable;
- yearly echo if the root is enlarging;
- referral to cardiology if dilation is significant. Growth of ≥0.5 cm in one year is considered rapid and an indication for intervention.

Follow local cardiology guidance where it exists.

instruction: You are a medical educator explaining research limitations and diagnostic challenges. Based on the article, why might the diagnosis rates of hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS) vary so much depending on the criteria used?
input: We found prevalence of hypermobile EDS according to different classifications in the same participants group at a decreasing prevalence; 19.4%, 15.2%, and 1.2%, respectively. Main reason for this may be the lack of features B in our populations, information about the syndrome in young people's families... The another reason may be the fact that with the 2017 International Classification criteria, the joint hypermobility and secondary musculoskeletal problems were not adequate for the definition of a genetic syndrome...
output: Diagnostic criteria can drastically change how many people are diagnosed with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS). In the study, when using older criteria (like Brighton or Villefranche), the prevalence seemed much higher (19.4% and 15.2%), but when applying the strict 2017 International Classification, it dropped to just 1.2%. This happens because newer criteria require not just flexible joints and pain, but also evidence involving other body systems (like specific connective tissue features) and often a known family history, which many young people might not be aware of yet.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'What genetic counseling and DNA-banking advice applies to patients with hEDS?' Answer based on the article.
input: Most individuals diagnosed with hEDS have an affected parent, although a detailed history and examination of the parents is often necessary to recognize that a parent has a current or prior history of joint laxity, easy bruising, and skin manifestations despite the absence of serious complications. Each child of an individual with hEDS has a 50% chance of inheriting hEDS. Family planning: It is appropriate to offer genetic counseling (including discussion of potential risks to offspring) to young adults who are affected. DNA banking: Because it is likely that testing methodology and our understanding of genes, pathogenic mechanisms, and diseases will improve in the future, consideration should be given to banking DNA from a proband diagnosed with hEDS. Hypermobile EDS is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner with variable expression of signs and variable severity of symptoms among affected family members.
output:
Offer genetic counseling to affected young adults, including discussion of the 50% risk to offspring under autosomal dominant inheritance with variable expression. Most probands have an affected parent, which may only become clear after a detailed family history and examination.

Because testing methods and understanding are likely to improve, consider banking DNA from the diagnosed proband.

instruction: A person going through diagnosis asks: 'My doctor tested my Beighton score. How is each point checked, and why could the result be wrong?' Answer based on the article.
input: Passive dorsiflexion of each fifth finger greater than 90 degrees. This should be assessed with the palm and forearm resting on a flat surface and is considered positive only if the fifth metacarpal-phalangeal joint (MCP) can be extended more than 90 degrees. Hyperextension of each knee greater than 10 degrees. This should be measured with a goniometer, with the individual standing and knees fully extended. Ability to place the palms flat on the floor with the knees fully extended. This should be assessed with the knees locked in extension and the feet together and is considered positive only if the total palm of both hands lies flat on the floor just in front of the feet. Slight flexion of the knees, spreading of the feet, failure to get the heels of the palms to the floor, and positioning the hands more than a few inches in front of the feet are common causes of false positive scoring of this point.
output: The Beighton score has 9 points, and the article stresses that each one should be checked in a standard way. For the little finger, your palm and forearm rest flat on a table, and the point counts only if the knuckle joint itself bends back more than 90 degrees. For the knee, you stand with knees fully straight and the overextension (more than 10 degrees) is measured with a goniometer, a joint-angle ruler. For the forward bend, knees must be locked straight and feet together, and your whole palms must lie flat on the floor just in front of your feet. Slightly bent knees, feet apart, heels of the hands not touching, or hands placed far in front can give a falsely positive point. Careful technique matters, so it's fine to ask how the test was done if the result surprises you.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'A hypermobile patient has had several low-trauma fractures. Can I attribute this to hEDS?' Answer based on the article.
input: Overall, there is no convincing evidence that hEDS is associated osteoporosis or fragility fractures, especially in children. Such persons should be evaluated for other underlying disorders. The bone fragility disorder, osteogenesis imperfecta, as well as the EDS/osteogenesis imperfecta overlap, have JH and may be mistaken for hEDS. In the above-mentioned studies, it is unclear if hEDS is associated with osteoporosis in adults, especially premenopausal women. There is no evidence at present to suggest that children or infants have a lower bone mass in hEDS nor that they are predisposed to fragility fractures.
output:
No. There is no convincing evidence that hEDS causes osteoporosis or fragility fractures, especially in children, and bone mineral density studies in adults are inconsistent. Lower activity levels may confound some findings.

Patients with fragility fractures should be evaluated for other disorders. Osteogenesis imperfecta and the EDS/OI overlap both cause joint hypermobility and can be mistaken for hEDS.

instruction: A patient with HSD asks: 'Can physiotherapy really help in the long run?' Answer based on the study.
input: After a standardized initial evaluation, all patients were offered the same coordinated physical therapy, were followed-up at 6 months and at least 1 year later, and were asked whether or not their condition had subjectively improved. At T2 (20 months) 54% of patients reported improvement (no difference between groups). On multivariable analysis, only family history of hypermobility predicted (favorable) outcome (p = 0.01). Perhaps, empowerment is facilitated by the presence of the disability in a parent or a child in the same family. Also, having another family member with the same diagnosis could induce motivation for rehabilitation.
output: The results are encouraging. In this study, patients with hEDS or HSD took part in a coordinated physiotherapy program and were followed for about 20 months. By then, 54% said their condition had improved, and the results were the same for hEDS and HSD. Interestingly, the only factor that predicted a better outcome was having a family history of hypermobility. The authors suggest this may be because having a relative with the same condition helps people feel more empowered and motivated to stick with rehabilitation.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A gastroenterologist asks: 'How should I approach the diagnostic workup of GI symptoms in a patient with hEDS/HSD?' Answer based on the AGA expert review.
input: Best Practice Advice 8: Diagnostic evaluation of GI symptoms consistent with DGBI in patients with hEDS/HSDs and comorbid POTS and/or MCAS should follow a similar approach to the evaluation of DGBI as in the general population including the use of a positive symptom-based diagnostic strategy and limited noninvasive testing. Best Practice Advice 9: Testing for celiac disease may be considered earlier in the diagnostic evaluation of patients with hEDS/HSDs who report a variety of GI symptoms and not only limited to those with diarrhea. There is insufficient research to support routine testing for disaccharidase deficiencies or other diet-mediated mechanisms as causes of GI symptoms in hEDS/HSDs. Best Practice Advice 10: Diagnostic testing for functional defecation disorders with anorectal manometry, balloon expulsion test, or defecography should be considered in patients with hEDS/HSDs and lower GI symptoms such as incomplete evacuation given the high prevalence of pelvic floor dysfunction, especially rectal hyposensitivity, in this population. Best Practice Advice 11: In patients with hEDS/HSDs and comorbid POTS who report chronic upper GI symptoms, timely diagnostic testing of gastric motor functions (eg, measurement of gastric emptying and/or accommodation) should be considered after appropriate exclusion of anatomical and structural diseases, as abnormal gastric emptying may be more common than in the general population.
output:
The AGA recommendations:

- General approach: evaluate DGBI as in the general population, using a positive, symptom-based diagnosis and limited noninvasive testing, even when POTS or MCAS coexist.
- Celiac disease: consider testing earlier, and not only in patients with diarrhea.
- Disaccharidase deficiencies and other diet-mediated mechanisms: routine testing is not supported by current evidence.
- Lower GI symptoms such as incomplete evacuation: consider anorectal manometry, balloon expulsion or defecography. Pelvic floor dysfunction, especially rectal hyposensitivity, is common in this population.
- Chronic upper GI symptoms with comorbid POTS: after excluding structural disease, consider timely gastric emptying and/or accommodation testing, since abnormal emptying may be more common.

The overall principle is targeted testing guided by the dominant symptoms rather than broad testing.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'How can pressure pain thresholds be measured reliably when assessing hyperalgesia?' Answer based on the study methods.
input: Thereupon, a blinded researcher assessed PPTs at 14 body locations on the trunk and extremities. The pressure was gradually increased at a rate of 1 kg/s until the subject indicated that the pain level has been reached. The threshold was determined as the mean of the 2 last values out of the 3 consecutive measurements.
output:
The study protocol:
- A blinded assessor used a pressure algometer at 14 sites on the trunk and extremities.
- Pressure was increased at 1 kg/s until the subject reported pain.
- Three consecutive measurements were taken at each site, and the threshold was the mean of the last two.

The authors note this method is efficient and reliable for exploring pain mechanisms. Including sites away from the painful areas allows generalized hyperalgesia to be detected.

instruction: You are a medical educator. Based on the article, how is the spine affected in hEDS?
input: Postural kyphosis is commonly encountered in those with hEDS. This is thought to be primarily due to loose ligamentous structure and poor postural ergonomics. Scoliosis is also common occurring in up to half of all patients. The scoliosis is acquired, often mild as well as flexible and may continue to progress beyond the adolescent period but most do not require intervention. Laxity of the lumbar spine increases movement and decreases stability. Young males with GJH had excessive lumbar segmental motion which was associated with increased low back pain, disability, and limited physical activity.
output: The spine is a chain of joints, so it can be affected too. A rounded upper back (postural kyphosis) is common, mainly because of loose ligaments and poor posture habits. Scoliosis—a sideways curve of the spine—occurs in up to half of people with hEDS. It usually develops over time, is mild and flexible, and although it may keep progressing slightly after adolescence, most people don't need treatment for it. In the lower back, extra looseness means more movement and less stability, which has been linked to more low back pain and reduced physical activity.

instruction: You are a health educator. Based on the qualitative study, how does living with JHS/hEDS affect people's lives emotionally and socially?
input: 17 participants (14 women, 3 men) purposively selected to broadly represent different genders, ages and ethnicities. Analysis identified five key themes: healthcare limitations, a lack of awareness of Joint Hypermobility and Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (Hypermobility Type) among healthcare professionals; a restricted life; social stigma; fear of the unknown; and ways of coping. Difficulty in keeping up with friends, family and colleagues led to feelings of frustration and anger in participants. Several described themselves as 'weird' or 'useless', experiencing shame. Not knowing when the next injury was going to occur or how their illness trajectory was going to affect them made participants especially fearful of future declines in their physical ability.
output: Interviews with 17 adults with JHS/hEDS showed that the condition affects much more than the joints. People described frustrations with healthcare and a lack of awareness among professionals; a life restricted by pain and fatigue; social stigma, including frustration and anger at not being able to keep up with friends, family or colleagues and sometimes feeling 'weird', 'useless' or ashamed; and fear of the unknown—not knowing when the next injury would happen or how the condition would affect their future. If you recognize these feelings, you are not alone, and they are worth raising with your care team.

instruction: A patient asks: 'I have rheumatoid arthritis. Can I also be diagnosed with hEDS?' Answer based on the article.
input: Criterion 3: All the following must be met: Absence of unusual skin, ocular, periodontal, vascular, or visceral organ tissue fragility or skeletal dysplasia, which should prompt consideration of other types of EDS. Exclusion of alternative diagnoses associated with joint hypermobility due to hypotonia and/or connective tissue laxity such as neuromuscular disorders, other heritable connective tissue disorders, and skeletal dysplasias. Other rheumatologic disorders may be the cause of musculoskeletal pain and inflammation (e.g., osteoarthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and rheumatoid arthritis); these disorders may coexist with hEDS. In individuals with a rheumatologic disorder, the diagnosis of hEDS requires that sufficient features in Criterion 2, Feature C are due to hEDS and not the co-occurring rheumatologic disorder.
output: Yes, it's possible—rheumatic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, lupus or osteoarthritis can exist alongside hEDS. But because they also cause joint pain and inflammation, the doctor has to be convinced that enough of your pain or joint instability comes from hEDS and not from the arthritis. More generally, the third hEDS criterion requires ruling out other explanations: unusual fragility of the skin, eyes, gums, blood vessels or internal organs, or abnormal bone development, would point to another type of EDS, and conditions such as neuromuscular diseases or other inherited connective tissue disorders must be excluded.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A physiotherapy service lead asks: 'Can standard rehabilitation protocols harm hypermobile patients?' Answer based on the review.
input: Strict protocols leave little flexibility for providers to take a holistic or creative approach or deviate from established care pathways. In some cases, this requirement can lead to poor outcomes in people with hEDS/HSD. For instance, 38% of participants in Bovet et al. (2016) reported iatrogenic injuries from rehabilitation care, including hyperextensions, torn ligaments, and dislocations, which the researchers attributed to 'physical therapists and other providers who adhered to standard treatment protocols without adjusting for patients' specific needs'.
output:
Yes. In one study, 38% of participants with hEDS/HSD reported iatrogenic injuries from rehabilitation, including hyperextensions, torn ligaments and dislocations. The researchers attributed these to clinicians adhering to standard protocols without adjusting for patients' specific needs.

Implications:
- Allow therapists flexibility to adapt protocols to the individual.
- Assess the whole patient, not only the presenting joint.
- Train staff in hypermobility.

instruction: A patient asks: 'I bruise and bleed easily. Is there any treatment?' Answer based on the article.
input: Hematologic. Platelet disorders may respond to tranexamic or mefenamic acid. For severe bleeding or operative prophylaxis, desmopressin acetate (DDAVP) may be beneficial. Micronutrient deficiencies may also be responsible for bleeding (e.g., low vitamin C) and anemia (e.g., folate and vitamin B12). Topical agents and adhesives should be used cautiously in those with skin fragility and/or allergy.
output: Yes, there are options. If bleeding is related to how platelets work, medicines such as tranexamic acid or mefenamic acid may help, and desmopressin (DDAVP) can be used for severe bleeding or to prevent bleeding during surgery. It's also worth checking for deficiencies: low vitamin C can contribute to bleeding, and low folate or vitamin B12 can cause anemia. If your skin is fragile, be careful with adhesive plasters, tapes and creams. Talk with your doctor, who may refer you to a hematologist, especially before any planned surgery.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'Where does generalized HSD fit in the hypermobility spectrum, and what should I expect in families?' Answer based on the review.
input: The HT-EDS phenotype significantly overlaps and is now thought to be clinically indistinguishable from joint hypermobility syndrome (JHS) and benign joint hypermobility syndrome (BJHS). In order to resolve this conundrum, a continuous spectrum of hypermobility was proposed. Patients who present with some mandatory features included in the hEDS criteria and those diagnosed with these phenotypically similar disorders can be classified as having 'Generalised Hypermobility Spectrum Disorder' (G-HSD), one of the 'Hypermobility Spectrum Disorders' (HSD) which reside in the middle of the spectrum. Individuals within the same pedigree may show different hypermobility phenotypes described in the spectrum.
output:
Hypermobility is viewed as a continuous spectrum. Generalized HSD (G-HSD) sits in the middle: patients have some of the mandatory features of hEDS, or carry older labels such as EDS hypermobility type, JHS or BJHS, which are now considered clinically indistinguishable.

Members of the same pedigree can show different phenotypes along the spectrum. When you evaluate relatives of a patient with hEDS, expect variable expression rather than identical presentations.

instruction: A patient recently diagnosed with hEDS asks: 'How do other people cope with this condition?' Answer based on the study.
input: Coping approaches identified included acceptance, building social networks, learning about joint hypermobility and adapting activities. Physiotherapists supported regular exercise. Physiotherapists with knowledge of Joint Hypermobility Syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome Hypermobility Type were cited as sources of support and hope, which helped people to cope with and manage their condition. The provision of reliable information and materials is vital, both for healthcare professionals and patients, to reduce misinformation and fear.
output: People in this study described several strategies that helped them cope: accepting the condition, building a network of supportive people, learning as much as possible about joint hypermobility, and adapting activities rather than giving them up. Regular exercise supported by a physiotherapist was important, and physiotherapists who understood hypermobility were described as real sources of support and hope. The authors also stress that reliable information matters—it helps reduce misinformation and fear, so it's worth choosing trustworthy sources.

instruction: A person going through diagnosis asks: 'What should I mention to my family doctor so they can consider hEDS?' Answer based on the article.
input: The symptoms most likely to raise the suspicion of a connective tissue disorder are not usually the symptoms that drive patients to primary care providers. Musculoskeletal injuries like joint dislocations, particularly if recurrent, might lead a provider to consider a connective tissue dysfunction. However, these acute injuries are usually encountered in the emergency department or an orthopedic specialty clinic, where chronic pain, fatigue, and other multisystem problems are not likely to be evaluated. When hEDS/HSD patients fail to respond to local or regional anesthetics, this is often discovered during dental procedures and not likely to be discussed in a primary care encounter. Multisystem symptoms, the most prominent of which are pain and fatigue, are likely attributed to conditions more familiar to primary care providers, such as fibromyalgia or chronic fatigue syndrome.
output: The article explains why hEDS is easily missed: the clues are scattered across different places. Dislocations are usually treated in the emergency department or by an orthopedist, local anesthetics not working is noticed at the dentist, and the family doctor mainly hears about pain and fatigue, which are then often attributed to fibromyalgia or chronic fatigue syndrome. So it helps to bring the whole picture together for your family doctor: past dislocations or subluxations (even if treated elsewhere), times when local anesthesia didn't work well, how flexible you were as a child, and other symptoms such as dizziness on standing, gut problems, easy bruising or slow-healing scars, as well as relatives with similar problems. A written list or timeline can make it easier to see the connections.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician performing procedures asks: 'What has gone wrong when patients with hEDS reported pain despite local anesthesia?' Answer based on the review.
input: A few participants reported particularly egregious behavior from providers. For example, two participants who were unresponsive to local anesthetics told how providers refused to believe they could still feel pain during a procedure: 'I could feel what they were doing. And I—I spoke up, and [the doctor] basically said, 'No, you can't.' and… carried on'. Another stated, 'I can still vividly remember the feeling of the thread [suturing] being pulled through my skin'.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'How should I classify joint hypermobility findings, and how does that relate to hEDS?' Answer based on the study.
input: Joint hypermobility were classified as generalized, peripheral and localized asymptomatic or hypermobility spectrum disorders. Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome was defined according to; 1) Brighton criteria... and 3) The 2017 International Classification of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
output:
Joint hypermobility can be classified as:
- generalized, peripheral or localized asymptomatic joint hypermobility;
- a hypermobility spectrum disorder (HSD) when it is symptomatic.

hEDS is a separate, syndromic diagnosis. This study defined it using three sets of criteria: Brighton, Villefranche and the 2017 International Classification.

In practice, first describe the pattern (generalized, peripheral or localized) and whether it causes symptoms. Then consider formal hEDS criteria only for symptomatic generalized hypermobility. The 2017 criteria are the current standard.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'What has fibroblast research revealed about the biology of hEDS?' Answer based on the article.
input: Classical (cEDS), vascular (vEDS), and hypermobile (hEDS) EDS are the most frequent types. cEDS and vEDS are caused respectively by defects in collagen V and collagen III, whereas the molecular basis of hEDS is unknown. These cells, though sharing a pathological ECM remodeling, show differences in the underlying pathomechanisms. In hEDS cells, gene expression changes related to cell-matrix interactions, inflammatory/pain responses, and acquisition of an in vitro pro-inflammatory myofibroblast-like phenotype may contribute to the complex pathogenesis of the disorder. Until now, no validated biological biomarkers have been identified for recognizing hEDS/HSD.
output:
Classical EDS is caused by collagen V defects and vascular EDS by collagen III defects, but the molecular basis of hEDS is unknown. Dermal fibroblasts from all three types show pathological extracellular matrix remodeling, through different mechanisms.

In hEDS fibroblasts, gene expression changes affect cell-matrix interactions and inflammatory and pain pathways, and the cells acquire a pro-inflammatory, myofibroblast-like phenotype in vitro. These findings may help explain pain and inflammation, but no validated biological biomarker yet exists for clinical diagnosis of hEDS or HSD.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'What are the consequences of attributing hEDS symptoms to psychosomatic causes?' Answer based on the study.
input: Another concern is that many individuals have had their symptoms dismissed as psychosomatic. Although these co-diagnoses only affected 16% of our population (82 individuals), such dismissal has critical negative consequences for the patient's psychological and physical well-being, potentially leading to a delayed diagnosis, the prescription of unnecessary antipsychotics, and the development of long-lasting trauma responses to otherwise benign clinical encounters. It is therefore unsurprising that functional neurologic disorders had the highest rejection rates (95%).

instruction: You are a health educator. Based on the article, why is sleep often poor in hEDS and why does it matter?
input: Sleep deprivation is considered unhealthy leading to fatigue, a decreased immune response, poor muscle coordination, susceptibility to injury, impaired cognition and memory, increased pain, moodiness, and depression. Sleep deprivation due to sleep maintenance insomnia has been related to impairment of the endogenous pain inhibitory function and therefore increases spontaneous pain and pain amplification. Many patients with hEDS report poor sleep including insomnia and unrefreshing sleep. In a study of 115 patients with hEDS, a significant decrease in sleep quality as compared to controls was found. Many other factors may also interfere with sleep in this population including pain, dysautonomia, poor sleep hygiene, and medications.
output: Many people with hEDS have trouble falling or staying asleep, or wake up unrefreshed; a study of 115 patients found clearly worse sleep quality than in healthy people. Pain, problems with the autonomic nervous system, medications and sleep habits can all interfere with sleep. This matters because poor sleep feeds into other symptoms: it worsens fatigue, coordination, memory and mood, increases the risk of injury, and weakens the body's own pain-control system, so pain feels stronger. Improving sleep is therefore an important part of managing hEDS.

instruction: A patient says: 'A doctor told me hypermobility doesn't cause pain and it's just the way I am.' Respond with empathy and accurate information based on the article.
input: All included studies attributed delayed diagnoses to the lack of provider knowledge. Other providers had limited, outdated, or incorrect understanding of the condition. Participants remembered their clinicians saying such things as, 'hypermobility shouldn't be causing pain, it's just the way you are', 'you're not hypermobile because you can't touch the floor', and, 'ooh the stretchy skin thing'. Many providers did not know that chronic widespread pain was a common hEDS/HSD characteristic, believing it was a benign condition with lax joints in otherwise healthy people. Also, there are few knowledgeable specialists to whom a provider can refer patients with suspected hEDS/HSD.
output: I'm sorry you heard that—it's a common and frustrating experience. Research on people with hEDS/HSD found that many clinicians have limited or outdated knowledge, and some still believe hypermobility is harmless and doesn't cause pain. In fact, chronic and widespread pain is one of the most common and important features of hEDS and HSD and is even part of the diagnostic criteria. Patients have also been told things like 'you can't be hypermobile because you can't touch the floor', even though flexibility often decreases with age. If you feel unheard, it's reasonable to ask for a referral to a clinician with experience in hypermobility, such as a clinical geneticist or a rheumatologist with an interest in this area—though the study notes such specialists can be hard to find.

instruction: You are a health educator discussing pelvic health. Based on the article, are bladder and pelvic floor problems more common in women with hEDS?
input: The largest prospective case-control study to date involved 120 women. Sixty women diagnosed with JHS, according to the Brighton criteria, were recruited from a tertiary referral hypermobility clinic, matched with healthy control women according to age, parity and ethnicity. The prevalence of UI in those with hEDS was significantly higher than in controls (73.3% vs. 48.3%) as was voiding difficulties. The impact of UI on QoL was also statistically significant. Objective findings of prolapse of the anterior vaginal wall were more severe than in controls. However, another recent study reported a lack of strong association of JH with UI or POP.
output: Probably yes, although the research is not completely consistent. In the largest careful study, 60 women with joint hypermobility syndrome were compared with 60 similar women of the same age and number of births. Urinary incontinence (leaking urine) affected 73.3% of the hypermobile women versus 48.3% of the others, difficulty emptying the bladder was also more common, and incontinence had a bigger effect on quality of life. Prolapse of the front vaginal wall was also more severe. However, another study did not find a strong link, so more research is needed. If you have bladder or pelvic floor symptoms, it is worth mentioning them—pelvic floor physiotherapy and other treatments can help.

instruction: You are a medical educator explaining clinical testing methods. How were pressure pain thresholds (PPTs) assessed in the study?
input: Thereupon, a blinded researcher assessed PPTs at 14 body locations on the trunk and extremities. The pressure was gradually increased at a rate of 1 kg/s until the subject indicated that the pain level has been reached. The threshold was determined as the mean of the 2 last values out of the 3 consecutive measurements.
output: Pressure pain thresholds (PPTs) were measured by a blinded researcher across 14 anatomical locations on the trunk and limbs. Pressure was increased at a steady rate of 1 kg/s until the participant signaled they reached their pain limit, and the threshold was calculated as the average of the final two out of three consecutive tests.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'How should ethnicity, age and sex influence my interpretation of joint hypermobility?' Answer based on the article.
input: The term 'joint hypermobility' refers to the ability of one or more joints to actively and/or passively move beyond normal limits. It may affect a few joints (i.e., monoarticular or localized JHM) or present in multiple body sites (i.e., generalized JHM). JHM is a sign, not a disease, and its occurrence varies by age, sex, and ethnicity. In fact, loose joints are more common among females and children than males and older people. By ethnicity, JHM is observed in up to 35-57% Africans, while it shows a much lower rate (6% in females, 2% in males) among Caucasians. In addition, various acquired/environmental factors, such as traumas, surgery, and regular training, may contribute in increasing range of motion at one or more joints.
output:
Joint hypermobility is a sign, not a disease. It is more common in females and children than in males and older people, and its prevalence varies by ethnicity: up to 35–57% in African populations, compared with about 6% of Caucasian women and 2% of Caucasian men. Trauma, surgery and regular training can also increase range of motion.

Interpret findings holistically. A high Beighton score in a young woman of African ancestry carries less diagnostic weight on its own than in an older Caucasian man. Distinguishing benign hypermobility from a heritable connective tissue disorder relies on associated symptoms and systemic features.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A physiotherapist asks: 'How does fatigue influence injury risk and exercise participation in hEDS?' Answer based on the article.
input: Fatigue may also be a factor in musculoskeletal pain and injury. Exercise to the point of physical fatigue has been shown to alter kinematics, postural stability, and coordination, which may increase the risk of direct injury and also the risk of falls causing secondary injury. A study of 30 EDS patients showed correlation between fatigue and objectively measured muscle weakness. Exercise-induced fatigue increases knee laxity, which may also increase the risk of knee injury. Fatigue is also associated with reduced ground reactive force during gait, suggestive of decreased proprioception, which could also increase the risk for falls and injury. Severity of fatigue also correlated with kinesiophobia in hEDS and, therefore, became an activity-limiting factor.
output:
Fatigue is a modifiable risk factor:
- Exercising to fatigue alters kinematics, postural stability and coordination, which increases the risk of direct injury and falls.
- Fatigue correlates with objectively measured muscle weakness.
- Exercise-induced fatigue increases knee laxity.
- Fatigue is associated with reduced ground reaction force during gait, which suggests impaired proprioception.
- More severe fatigue correlates with kinesiophobia, which limits activity.

Practical implications: dose exercise below the point of exhaustion, include proprioceptive training, monitor fatigue during programs, and address fear of movement explicitly.

instruction: You are a medical educator. Based on the article, do people with hEDS have weak bones or osteoporosis?
input: Overall, there is no convincing evidence that hEDS is associated osteoporosis or fragility fractures, especially in children. Such persons should be evaluated for other underlying disorders. The bone fragility disorder, osteogenesis imperfecta, as well as the EDS/osteogenesis imperfecta overlap, have JH and may be mistaken for hEDS. In the above-mentioned studies, it is unclear if hEDS is associated with osteoporosis in adults, especially premenopausal women. There is no evidence at present to suggest that children or infants have a lower bone mass in hEDS nor that they are predisposed to fragility fractures.
output: According to current evidence, hEDS has not been convincingly linked to osteoporosis or to bones that break easily, especially in children. Research in adults is mixed and inconclusive, partly because people with hEDS are often less physically active, which itself lowers bone density. If a child or adult with hypermobility has fractures after minor trauma, doctors should look for other causes—for example osteogenesis imperfecta ('brittle bone disease'), which also causes loose joints and can be mistaken for hEDS.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'Which Beighton cut-off defines generalized joint hypermobility in adults, and how much does the choice matter?' Answer based on the study.
input: Results: In total, 77.3% (n=259) of participants had any class of joint hypermobility and 25.9% (n=87) of them had generalized class. Generalized joint hypermobility was defined in participants firstly as a Beighton scoring of >=4/9... and secondly with Beighton scoring >=5/9.
output:
This study defined generalized joint hypermobility in two ways: a Beighton score of 4 or more out of 9, and a score of 5 or more out of 9. With these definitions, 25.9% of healthy 18–25-year-old students had generalized hypermobility, and 77.3% had some class of hypermobility.

The cut-off strongly affects how many people are classified as hypermobile, so always state which threshold you used.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. An obstetrician asks: 'Does joint hypermobility affect delivery outcomes or later pelvic floor disorders?' Answer based on the article.
input: A large study was conducted to investigate the association between JH, obstetrical outcomes, and pelvic floor disorders [Knoepp et al., 2013]. It involved 587 parous women. JH and pelvic floor disorders were evaluated at enrollment (5–10 years after first delivery). The researchers defined JH as Beighton score ≥4 and did not use the Brighton or Villefranche criteria. JH was diagnosed in 46 women (7.8%) and was associated with decreased odds of caesarean after complete cervical dilation or operative vaginal delivery. In this study, anal sphincter laceration was less likely to occur in women with JH and was not associated with any pelvic floor disorder. Although this study did not address the issues related to hEDS specifically, the results are quite reassuring for women with asymptomatic hypermobility as JH seem to facilitate spontaneous vaginal birth but does not appear to be a risk factor for pelvic floor disorders in the first decade after childbirth.

instruction: You are a medical educator. Based on the article, explain how stretch marks in hEDS differ from what people might expect, including during pregnancy.
input: Striae atrophicae often appear during the adolescent growth spurt usually between the ages of 11-13 years and not necessarily associated with rapid weight gain; however, this can also be seen in adolescents without an underlying connective tissue disorder as well. By contrast, striae gravidarum may be minimal or nonexistent in some as skin of the mature hEDS female is inherently stretchy so that the elastic limit is never reached despite the enlarging maternal abdomen.
output: In hEDS, stretch marks often appear during the growth spurt around ages 11-13, even without fast weight gain—although teenagers without a connective tissue disorder can get them too. Surprisingly, some women with hEDS get very few or no stretch marks during pregnancy. Their skin is naturally stretchier, so it may never reach its limit even as the belly grows.

instruction: A patient asks: 'Why did it take so many years for me to get diagnosed with hEDS?' Answer based on the review.
input: The reviewers identified and organized diagnosis delay themes under four overarching categories: disease, patient, provider, and system. Disease factors included the nature of the symptoms and lack of a confirmatory test. Patient factors included psychological and emotional responses, seeing multiple providers, and receiving multiple diagnoses. Provider factors related to limited knowledge and attitudes. System factors included silo-based health care systems and bureaucratic barriers.
output: Unfortunately, long delays are very common, and they usually have several overlapping causes. This review grouped them into four areas. The disease: symptoms are varied and subtle, and there's no confirming test. The patient's journey: emotional responses, seeing many different providers and collecting multiple diagnoses along the way. Healthcare providers: many have limited knowledge of hEDS, and some have dismissive attitudes. The healthcare system: care split into separate specialties that don't talk to each other, plus bureaucratic hurdles. None of this was your fault.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'How should refractory reflux, gastritis and other GI problems be managed in hEDS?' Answer based on the article.
input: Gastritis and gastroesophageal reflux disease may require intensive therapy, including proton pump inhibitor twice daily before meals, high-dose H2 blocker at bedtime, sucralfate, and over-the-counter acid-neutralizing agents. Other treatable causes such as H pylori infection and small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) should be investigated and treated. Upper endoscopy is indicated for resistant symptoms, but frequently is normal. Delayed gastric and colonic emptying should be identified and treated, as should causes of anorectal pain and prolapse.
